The fiscal space within the debt rule/ PSNFL rule can be increased if instruments used to boost capital spending include some financial assets (loans and equity stakes) that can be netted against debt in the PSNFL rule. This can be done via public financial institutions (PuFins) such as the National Wealth Fund or National Housing Bank, which use public money to provide loans and equity investments to the private sector. records.text: 1M/36M timespread has risen by $30/bbl year-to-date (or by 42pp), challenging the historically strong relationship between OECD commercial stocks and the Brent 1M/36M timespread. In a large sample starting in 1998, OECD commercial stocks in days of demand are able to explain over 60% of the variation in the timespread (Exhibit 3, left panel). The explanatory power of OECD commercial stocks has edged down over the last couple of years, in part because market attention has broadened to oil stocks outside the OECD region amid increasing data availability and quality (Exhibit 3, right panel). As global landed oil stocks outside OECD commercial storage have become more predictive of prices, our fair value model now includes them as well. Although large data sets (e.g. Kpler satellite-based global crude stocks) on global visible oil stocks outside the OECD became available only after 2017, we still estimate our timespread fair-value model using a sample starting in 1998, to capture the largest and longest possible dataset. records.text: 4 US Economic Weekly | 09 October 2026 What would an Oct pause mean for the Fed outlook? If the Fed pauses in Oct, we think the most likely policy path would be two more 25bp hikes, in Dec 2026 and Mar 2027. However, the risks to that outlook would be two sided. On the one hand, by moving slower the Fed might end up having to do more. So we wouldn’t rule out additional hikes in Jun and perhaps even Sep 2027. On the other hand, if y/y core inflation were to roll off due to favorable base effects next year, the Fed might stop after just one more hike in Dec 2026. In this scenario, the Fed’s caution would be vindicated. We think markets might even test the Fed’s resolve to hike in Dec. At the moment they are pricing just about one full hike by Dec. But pricing could come off meaningfully if we get soft jobs or inflation data and the Fed doesn’t clearly guide markets toward a hike. We’re sticking with our call for a hike in Oct for now, but we’ll re-assess next week after the September inflation data and Chair Warsh’s comments at the IMF meetings on Thursday.

records.text: ted as current or day-to-day spending. Second, there are maturity losses or gains . These occur when a bond is held until redemption (passive unwind). At this point, the APF receives the redemption value of the bond from the bond issuer (in most cases the government). This redemption value is often different from the price the APF paid for the bond initially – the initial proceeds amount – and the difference between these two is the maturity loss/gain. At the point when the APF initially buys the bond, the government can anticipate the future maturity loss (or gain), and so for all bonds purchased the difference between the purchase value and the redemption value is recognised on the government’s balance sheet upfront through an adjustment in the level of public sector debt (PSND). This means that when the loss is actually realised when the bond matures, there is no additional shift in PSND or Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities (PSNFL), an alternative measure of debt. 11 October 2026 3 Barclays | UK Themes

Introduction In response to the financial crisis of 2008 and subsequent shocks, the Bank of England, along with other global central banks, bought significant quantities of government bonds, in a policy known as quantitative easing (QE). records.text: FX and Rates: Stronger external support, limited domestic reflation Mitul Kotecha(i) Barclays Bank, Singapore China’s AI expansion presents an unusual combination: a positive growth and export shock that is unlikely to generate significant domestic reflation. Unlike in the US, where the AI build- out is supporting a broad investment cycle and adding to demand for capital, power and labour, China’s growth dividend comes primarily through exports. China’s large manufacturing base is capturing growing global demand for servers, data- processing equipment, AI-enabled consumer electronics, semiconductors, cooling systems and energy-storage equipment. AI-related investment is also increasing, but remains too small relative to total investment to offset fully the weakness in property and traditional infrastructure. This distinction is important for both China FX and rates. For the CNY, the rise in AI-related exports strengthens China’s trade and current-account position, providing an additional source of underlying support for the currency. For rates, however, stronger AI-related production does not necessarily imply a higher domestic policy-rate path. The export impulse has yet to translate into broad job creation, wage growth or household demand, while AI adoption in manufacturing and services is primarily improving productivity and reducing labour intensity. Luca Salford, Maria Chiara Russo, Jasper Knyphausen Our modelling points towards a 10y France-Germany spread above 200bp for TPI intervention based on the current information set. However, we think considerations about the speed of spread widening, the level of German bond yields, the extent of spillovers into other markets, and the macro and political context will also matter in the decision. How much can spreads still widen until the ECB intervenes in some shape or form? While, at the time of writing, the idea of a rescue intervention is being dismissed even by Banque de France Governor Moulin, we try to estimate a hypothetical range based on historical data at which intervention becomes far more likely. As a starting point, we view the problem through the lens of the ECB: there is a spread level that is justified by fundamentals such as the (expected) debt-to-GDP ratio, credit rating, or (expected) budget balance, to name just a few key factors. If spreads trade within that range, the ECB is unlikely to intervene. Beyond that, there is probably a level that is no longer justified purely by macroeconomic variables but would likely still be tolerated by the ECB, for example, because the resulting tightening in financial conditions is not yet impairing monetary policy transmission and there is little evidence that problems arising from the sovereign-bank nexus are becoming systemic. This undermines the economics of processing imported crude and raises the risk of refinery run cuts, particularly at less complex facilities with limited flexibility to adjust their crude slate. This is arguably the worst possible time to cut refinery runs, with global product markets already severely constrained, diesel inventories near historic lows and the Northern Hemisphere entering the peak winter demand season. The adjustment may therefore come not from an increase in tanker availability, but from a reduction in demand for tankers. If freight costs rise beyond what refiners can economically absorb, refinery runs and crude purchases will eventually decline, easing pressure on vessel demand. In that sense, the freight market may be approaching its own economic ceiling: not because the shortage of ships has been resolved, but because the cost of moving crude is becoming too high for refiners to bear. Still, qualitatively the assessment remains, the ECB's monetary policy stance is significantly tighter than what is implied by the actual policy rate increases. So if the increase in euro area long rates continues at the present speed, we could soon be reaching a situation in which the ECB wonders whether the tightening went too far too quickly. So, what should the ECB do? Cutting rates is not an option, as it needs to keep the tightening bias in place given the upside risks to the inflation outlook. But there is a far more elegant solution available: the ECB can, temporarily at least, stop QT. Such a decision would mean the ECB starts again reinvesting maturing government bonds. This should help limit the upward pressure on yields. The justification is simple and lies squarely within the realm of monetary policy: the observed tightening through the increase in long rates goes beyond what the ECB sees as needed at this stage. A more measured pace of tightening is in order. In such a situation, improving the degree of control over financial conditions takes precedence over the aim of reducing the size of the balance sheet. And here another coincidence comes in handy: Excess liquidity is close to a critical threshold of EUR 2 trillion (see here), so pausing QT would not come at a bad moment. records.text: /Bund spread sits at ~135bp, and the models broadly agree that a significant part of this is justified from a debt sustainability perspective, while roughly ~20–30bp reflects cheapness in OATs that cannot be explained by fundamentals. By historical comparison, residuals of roughly ~70– 100bp relative to fundamentally justified levels have been tolerated to some extent by the ECB without intervention, or at least have not led to a collapse of the bank-sovereign nexus. Based on these findings alone, the OAT/Bund spread would still have room to widen by around ~40–80bp before we might see any form of intervention. This would imply spread levels of roughly ~175–205bp. However, we also want to highlight several factors that could play a decisive role here, complicating the picture. First, we acknowledge that a target on the 10y spread is a simplification. From a market perspective, the speed of widening and how much short-term spreads are widening add to the picture. From this point of view, we find last week's price action concerning to the ECB regardless to the level of the 10y spread. Second, market instability can be both a function of the level of country spreads and the level of risk-free rates. In the current environment, risk-free rates well above recent historical levels might be problematic. As highlighted in previous pieces, we believe the global rates sell off in September exacerbated the widening of French spreads. Higher yields might thus warrant earlier action ceter

Our baseline forecast includes two rises in the coming months, with the first increase likely to come as soon as November, just one week after the Budget. Energy Core goods Food The energy shock continues to loom over the outlook. Oil prices remain higher than we had assumed in our midyear outlook as shipping costs have soared, and product prices are even higher. Global goods inflation is set to jump sharply as energy, food, and underlying core are all on the rise (Figure 3). The jump in energy costs will be immediately felt through a drag on purchasing power, adding to the importance for labor markets to rebound to help cushion the drag. The expected rise in core goods inflation, driven by surging tech prices and passthrough of energy costs, is likely more of a concern for central banks—which continued to signal a hawk- ish mood in this week's Fed and ECB minutes and BoJ quar- terly report. We look for a firm US headline September CPI report (0.55%) but another soft core print (0.18%). Financial conditions remain supportive, although some points of stress are visible. Although corporate and household debt accumulation is rising, leverage remains remarkably low. More concerning is the health of public sector finances, but while pressures have built in France, we see few similarities to 2012 and expect a credible budget and constructive com- ments from key presidential candidates to cool market fears (here and here). Real GDP grows 2.4% (4Q/4Q) in 2026 and 2.3% in 2027. Final private domestic demand is even stronger but slows modestly into next year. Labor: Low hire, low fire. Employment growth remains soft, but immigration controls have reduced breakevens to around 50k per month. The unemployment rate remains low. Inflation: A sticky path lower. We expect disinflation, but second round effects from the oil shock and residual seasonality mean slow progress. Core PCE ends 2026 at 3.0% (4Q/4Q) and 2027 at 2.6%. Consumer: Two-speeds. Low-income consumers remain squeezed, while wealth supports the high-end. Real consumption slows to 1.8% in 2027 from 2.3% in 2026. AI: Increasingly macro-relevant. AI-related investment contributes around 60bps to real GDP growth in 2026 and 2027. AI-driven productivity growth adds a further boost. Modest labor displacement. Fed: Measured tightening. We expect two 25bp hikes in December and March, to a target range of 4.25% - 4.5%. Data support a measured recalibration of Fed policy over more aggressive tightening.

Fiscal policy Government spending is an important component of demand in the economy. We expect to see reduced growth in total demand coming from this channel in the coming years, if the Chancellor sticks to plans to consolidate the public finances and reduce borrowing. Our baseline forecast includes already-announced policies, rather than assumptions about what will be announced in the Budget. For the variant that underpins the fiscal estimates made in the IFS Green Budget 2026, we also strip out policies announced since the last fiscal event – such as the cost-of-living measures announced over the summer – to more cleanly approximate the process undertaken by the OBR in producing its pre-measures forecast. The latest in-year data show that government has borrowed £77.3 billion so far this financial year (from April to August 2026), roughly £8 billion above the OBR’s expectation in its March forecast for borrowing up to this point (Office for National Statistics, 2026c). The current budget deficit – the difference between day-to-day spending and revenues –– was £51.9 billion over the same period, and £4.8 billion larger than the OBR had forecast. These misses are small in the scheme of large fiscal numbers though and do not change the overall fiscal narrative from March. records.text: FactSet Revere Business Industry Classification System (RBICS) and GS sectoral AI exposure estimates RBICS is a multi-sector classification framework designed to reveal a company’s true sector exposures by analyzing its primary and ancillary revenue streams. In essence, it normalizes non-standardized business segment reports, mapping companies’ segment revenues to granular sectors. The RBICS matrix structure consists of 12 anchor sectors, 6 levels of depth, and over 1,800 individual sector groups at the most granular sector level. This results in a quantified multi-sector participation tree for each company, enabling easy comparison, screening, and grouping. This revenue-based approach makes RBICS an effective tool in providing high visibility into a company’s business operations, and enabling investors to screen for firms with specific revenue exposure to specific AI-related activities. We apply the RBICS framework on all Chinese listed companies (~7,000), among which, we identify 3,170 names that spread across 249 RBICS sub-industries that are directly related or adjacent to the extended AI value chain per GS top-down and bottom-up assumptions. The notional-weighted with trend version adds long trend exposure by hedging the delta on the long legs only when it exceeds a certain absolute level. Pages 6–20 provide further detail on the various versions and present a series of charts and tables to help in the analysis and comparison of the different implementations across regions. The volatility premium (via short gamma exposure) has been a strong source of additional returns over the long term. This premium has increased in the current environment of higher inflation in Europe and the US, which is favorable for the notional-weighted versions. We believe conditions remain favorable despite the recent rise in realized volatility, which has been accompanied by an increase in implied volatility (see Figures 8, 9, 10, and 11 on pages 8 and 12). records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 09 October 2026 11 Risks for the market are that 1) the government aims for a small headroom number 2) Potential fiscal consolidation to restore the headroom is completely backloaded 3) the government uses the flexibility within the fiscal rules to increase investment spending by a large amount, raising gilt issuance more than expected. 4) Any carve outs or changes to the fiscal rules. In our base case we don’t expect any changes to fiscal rules or any carve-outs or exclusions. But one risk that exists is that government tweaks the debt rule to exclude public corporations borrowing to allow it more space to invest. Pre-measures headroom hit by £14bn to ~£10bn In March, the OBR estimated that the Chancellor has left a buffer against the stability rule (i.e. current budget in balance by 2029-30) of £23.6bn. The stability rule is currently the binding rule, and thereby the headroom was £23.6bn in March. The buffer against the debt rule (i.e public sector net financial liabilities to fall as a share of GDP by 2029- 30) was £26.5bn in March. Developments since March imply that the Chancellor’s pre-measures current budget headroom is likely to fall well below £23.6bn. Higher yields, Bank Rate expectations, inflation along weaker growth and potential migration downgrades are likely to lower the headroom, while some offsets are likely from higher asset prices and wage growth. We think the pre-measures headroom has been lowered by ~£14bn to ~£10bn from £23.6bn

records.text: ustralia’s housing downturn is expected to weigh on economic activity and inflation through 2027, but strong household balance sheets should help limit financial stability risks. Years of rising house prices have left households with substantial equity and liquidity buffers, with assets now worth more than six times liabilities and most mortgage borrowers holding sufficient savings to weather higher interest rates. As a result, the expected 10% decline in house prices is unlikely to trigger widespread financial stress, even though it should gradually dampen consumer spending through negative wealth effects, weaker housing turnover, softer dwelling investment, tighter small-business credit conditions and lower state government revenues. We estimate a 10% fall in house prices lowers consumption by 1.3%, with most of the effect emerging from 4Q-26. These housing-related headwinds, combined with weakening demand and easing labour market conditions, are expected to slow growth and inflation sufficiently to support an RBA shift toward a neutral policy stance in early 2027, ahead of interest rate cuts later that year. While we previously had a slight preference for IG vs. HY, we now view the case for an outright overweight in IG as less obvious based on valuations, rate sensitivity and supply related technicals. AI enables factories to produce more with fewer workers, particularly in routine assembly, quality control, logistics, and administrative functions. As a result, the number of manufacturing workers in China in 2025 was roughly 30% below its 2013 peak. In other words, AI is boosting productivity and output, but not generating enough new jobs to offset the broader decline in manufacturing employment. • Services. The same is true in services. Most corporate AI adoption is concentrated in customer service, back-office operations, coding assistance, financial processing, marketing, and document review, where the primary goal is to automate routine tasks and reduce headcount, not expand payrolls. While AI is creating some high-skilled jobs in software engineering, data science, model development, and cloud infrastructure, the numbers are too small to offset broader weakness in white-collar hiring. For context, China's entire IT sector, the industry most directly linked to AI, employs only around 8 million workers, less than 1.5% of total employment. The employment base is simply too small to move the needle for the overall labor market. More importantly, AI has yet to become a major job creator, even within the AI ecosystem itself. RIBA The look ahead: some drawdown as energy shock bites The UK economic story this year has been impressive, outpacing consensus expectations all year long. That said, with the UK economy running at a near 2% annualised GDP pace, we think some course correction remains likely. Questions around residual seasonality linger, with growth tending to outpace expectations in the first half of the year for some time now. The upcoming Blue Book revisions could temper this – and will be important to watch on 15 October. Where to next? Some slowdown in activity remains our base case. We expect September GDP to remain weak, leaving quarterly output expanding at a still stellar pace of 0.5% q -o-q. Thereafter, we expect growth to slow more meaningfully to 0.1% q -o-q, as more of the energy shock catches up with households and businesses. Budget uncertainty is likely to rear its head again. And we now think that tighter financial conditions will be validated by a modest tightening cycle by the Bank of England. Altogether, we expect annual GDP this year to rise by 1.4%, before pushing up by 1.5% in 2027 and 1.6% in 2028. Figure 12: UK atop the G7 league table

records.text: y and the Asset Purchase Facility? There are three direct ways that the QE/QT programme affects the public finances. All of these involve cash flows between HM Treasury and the Bank, but they have different effects on the fiscal aggregates (such as measures of government spending and debt). First, there is the interest rate loss or gain . This is the coupon payments the APF receives for the bonds it owns, minus the interest it pays to the Bank on the loan it used to finance the purchases (on which it is charged the Bank Rate). For a long time the APF was making a profit as the coupon payments it received from its bond holdings averaged 3-4% of their purchase cost and Bank Rate was at ultra-low levels of 0.5% or less. From 2012 onwards, this interest rate gain was sent each quarter to HM Treasury. The decision to send these profits immediately to HM Treasury was a policy choice; the government and the Bank could instead have agreed to keep those profits within the APF’s portfolio to cover potential future losses. More recently, this interest rate channel has turned negative. Bank Rate has risen (and is expected to rise further) while the coupon payments on the bonds have remained unchanged. Each quarter the government sends payments to the APF to cover this loss and these are counted as current or day-to-day spending. Second, there are maturity losses or gains . These occur when a bond is held until redemption (passive unwind). At this point, the APF receives the redemption va

Recent Bank of England announcements on the QT programme Helpfully, at its annual review of the QT programme in September, the Bank of England resolved much of the uncertainty around this path, publishing a multi-year outline of what it plans to do.3 This gives us greater certainty and allows us to model more confidently what the fiscal flows will be. The Bank of England explicitly stated it plans to actively sell £20 billion of government bonds each year for the next eight years, £12 billion a year less than the OBR had assumed in March. Furthermore, it announced that it would not sell any bonds that are set to mature after 2049. Instead, these long-dated bonds will be held and used as a long-term asset to back up the Bank of England’s bank note liability. This matters particularly for the public finances as it is these long-dated bonds which tend to incur the largest losses when sold. It will also refrain from selling any bonds that are set to mature before 2035. These will be held until they naturally mature and passively unwind. This means that all of the sales will be concentrated in bonds that would otherwise mature between 2035 and 2049, as opposed to the previous policy of selling across the entirety of the portfolio. The US and France are now in the spotlight, but the argument applies to Japan, the UK and other European countries. We argue that time inconsistent fiscal policies are at the root of the problem, exposing debt dynamics to multiple equilibria. Policymakers will have a tough time coordinating into the good equilibrium unless politicians show resolve to swallow the bitter medicine. Over the last 20 years, debt/GDP increased by about 50pp and 60pp of GDP for France and the US, respectively. Most of that increase took place during the ultra-low interest rates period. The problem is not only excessive borrowing during the low-rate era, but the political inability to adjust fiscal policy when the financing conditions that accommodated those deficits disappear. Much higher debt levels coupled with political dysfunctionality make debt sustainability substantially more sensitive to the real interest rate-growth differential (r-g). records.text: licial economy of fiscal deficits The central aspect relies on the time inconsistency of fiscal policies, both on the revenue and spending side. When interest rates are low, government have incentives to run bigger deficits financed with cheap debt. This is particularly attractive when the cost of financing is lower than the rate of growth of the economy (r < g). However, if that “cheap” debt goes to finance permanent increases/decreases in government spending/revenue, when interest rates increase it is politically difficult to implement the necessary fiscal consolidation to put the house in order. Before politicians decide to pay the political cost of reducing spending or increasing taxes, everything may be tried, from financial repression to debt monetization. The history of EM is rich in examples. The fiscal adjustment to changing financial conditions is asymmetric: spending commitments and tax reductions are politically easier to introduce or preserve than to reverse. As interest rates normalize, the debt stabilizing primary balance deteriorates, yet political resistance prevents fiscal policy for adjusting accordingly. France, the US and Japan as leading examples France exemplifies the rigidity of public spending coupled with the fragility of the revenue base. The US illustrates the massive share of entitlements and defense spending, which adds to around 70% of total public spending, with the political persistence of tax reductions. France and TPI in 2024: The TPI came into focus relative to France already in June 2024 around the announcement of snap parliamentary elections in France. At that time, the OAT-Bund spread widened by about 35bp. The ECB at the time was paying attention and highlighted that TPI is an important tool in ECB's toolkit, but did not see anything warranting a discussion on its use then (see Lane and Lagarde). Looking at the wider spreads of other euro area countries, the Governing Council was actually concerned that spreads at the time had become too tight and investors potentially too complacent (see here). So, back then, the re-widening of spreads to some extent addressed these concerns. Is the set-up different this time around? We don't think so (at least for now), and we think our framework from 2024 still applies (see here). Bond spreads not at the levels warranting TPI: Our most often asked question from investors so far has been: what level qualifies as "unwarranted widening" and hence TPI activation? One way to approach this question is to look back to 2022 to try to understand the ECB reaction function around TPI introduction. The BTP-Bund spread was closing in on 250bp at various times throughout 2022, and the ECB only engaged in verbally reassuring the market that the TPI has a firm place in its toolkit. A diagnosis of a severe distortion in the transmission would be needed to activate the TPI, rather than "just" a significant widening of the OAT-Bund spread. There are several avenues that could lead to ECB policy action. First, if we start to see similar spread widening in other countries, this could be seen as reflecting cross-market spillovers rather than changes in their domestic fundamentals. The spread widening in these countries could be viewed as unwarranted. In the extreme, it is conceivable to see the ECB using the TPI to limit adverse implications for the transmission of its policy by activating the TPI for all affected sovereigns – except for the Member State from which tensions originate, in this case, France. Second, the equity performance of the banking sector is also key, as it could have implications on the willingness of the banking sector to lend. This would have potential implications for the transmission of the ECB's monetary policy. While this would not be an immediate reaction, pressure could emerge in bank funding markets. If the same process had seemed to be dictated by HM Treasury in order to make fiscal savings, this could have been perceived as fiscal policy encroaching on the independence of the Bank of England. A second possible way to reduce the fiscal burden of the APF in coming years would be to reduce the compensation offered on central bank reserves. This is the cost part of the profit and loss equation. If the Bank no longer paid interest on reserves held by commercial banks then there would be scope for the APF to stop paying interest on its loan from the Bank, removing interest losses. Other economies have tried this on a limited scale, reducing the interest they pay on a fraction of the balances held with them in reserves. As a result, AI affects the Chinese economy through different channels than it does in the US. In this report, we quantify AI's impact on growth, employment, and inflation. Our key conclusion is that AI is already providing a meaningful boost to China's growth outlook. Without AI-related tailwinds, we estimate China's GDP growth would fall below 4% this year. We think the growth dividend comes primarily through exports rather than domestic investment, as China increasingly serves as the manufacturing hub of the global AI boom. The smaller scale of AI investment in China relative to the US does not reflect a lack of enthusiasm. Rather, it is being shaped by factors such as AI monetization, cash flow dynamics, and constraints on access to high-end chips (see Asia Credit Alpha: Funding the (AI) build, 8 Oct 2026). At the same time, our three-sector analysis suggests that AI is not creating enough jobs in China yet. While it is generating employment in data centres and AI-related high-tech manufacturing, the scale remains too small to offset larger job losses elsewhere. The property downturn remains a major drag on construction employment, while manufacturing firms are using AI and automation to reduce labor intensity. Putting AI into potential growth model In the longer term, the bigger opportunity from AI lies in productivity growth rather than cyclical demand support. Its main contribution comes through higher total factor productivity (TFP), as firms use AI to automate routine tasks, and improve efficiency across manufacturing and services. The IMF estimates that AI could lift global potential growth by as much as 1pp over five years, equivalent to an average annual boost of 0.2pp, with the gains increasing as generative AI adoption becomes more widespread. However, while AI may slow the decline in potential growth, it is unlikely to fully reverse it. To gauge the impact, we rely on a standard Cobb-Douglas production function framework: Y(t)=A(t)*K(t)α*(L(t)H(t))1-α. Where: Y = real GDP , A = total factor productivity (TFP), K = capital stock, L = number of employees, H = human capital, α = elasticity of output to capital, 1-α = elasticity of output to labour, and t = years. With a faster-shrinking and aging population, and diminishing returns to capital accumulation, we expect China's potential growth to continue trending lower despite AI- driven productivity gains. In our baseline scenario, AI, automation and machine learning provide some measured boost to TFP growth, partially offsetting demographic and investment headwinds. Even so, we expect potential growth to slow to approximately 2.5% 8 October 2026 6 Barclays | China AI Watch

We think we are still very far from the point the ECB would put the TPI even on the agenda of the Governing Council. We heard from Council members this week (and could also read in the accounts of the September meeting), that the spread widening was seen as justified by fundamentals. So, absent a significant further spread widening and clear signs of stress in funding markets for French banks, the ECB is unlikely to contemplate any action here. And even then, it will very likely want to see some political signals suggesting more consolidation efforts are under way. What is TPI? Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) was introduced in 2022, at the time of BTP-Bund spread widening, as the ECB's newest tool to address a distorted transmission mechanism (see description here). The essence of the tool is that the ECB can buy ex-ante unlimited quantities of euro area government bonds if it detects a spread widening and market dynamics that impair the transmission of its monetary policy and that are not warranted by fundamentals. Source: Barclays Research. Another potential route from the energy price shock to broad inflation is through the labour market. Workers might respond to the increase in prices they face by demanding higher wages to compensate, and firms might finance these higher wages through raising their own prices. This mechanism – often termed second-round effects or, at the extreme, a ‘wage–price spiral’ – could transmit the energy price shock out into the broader economy. However, our view is that this is unlikely to happen in a meaningful way in this instance due to the relatively weak demand for labour in the economy currently, as we discuss in The labour market, below. This weak demand relative to the supply of workers looking for jobs means workers have less bargaining power in wage negotiations. This point is illustrated by Figure 6, which shows the historical relationship between firms’ expectations of wages and of inflation, and how this has broken down since the conflict in the Middle East began. Since March, wage expectations have been insensitive, even as inflation expectations have moved. Because of these conditions, in our baseline scenario we expect limited scope for pressures from the labour market to push up inflation more broadly. 11 October 2026 6 Barclays | UK Economic Outlook

Broadly, we find that Treasury and credit curves have tended to move in opposite directions, with steeper Treasury curves often associated with flatter credit curves, particularly during bear-steepening episodes under a strong growth backdrop. Tactically, if rates remain flat to higher from current levels, we think it could support flatter credit curves in certain sectors that have historically been a large share of the longer-end of IG markets, such as Consumer Staples, Financials, and non-AI Industrials which have a bigger share of non-discretionary issuance that can be deferred or shifted further up the curve. However, Technology may prove the exception and still see steeper credit curves from here, since hyperscalers and other AI-related borrowers face substantial committed investment requirements and have less flexibility to reduce issuance simply because financing costs have risen. We are already seeing early evidence of this divergence playing out: non-hyperscaler 10s30s curves have flattened modestly since Jackson Hole, while hyperscaler curves have remained broadly unchanged over the same period. records.text: Updating our outlook for US equity issuance The pace of US equity issuance slowed sharply in Q3 following a record quarter in Q2. US corporates raised $93 billion of equity in Q3. This issuance reflected growth of 20% on a year/year basis but a steep decline from the record $252 billion of equity issuance in Q2. Follow-ons represented the bulk of issuance in Q3, totaling $45 billion, and IPOs raised just $7 billion. While half of the Q2 dollar issuance was concentrated in just two deals, the number of offerings also slowed materially in Q3 relative to Q2. September’s total of 19 follow-ons and 5 IPOs registered the lowest monthly counts in each category since the tariff shock in April 2025. Despite the sequential slowdown in issuance during Q3, IPO and follow-on proceeds in 2026 are on track to register the largest total since the boom of 2021. Year to date, equity issuance proceeds have totaled roughly $430 billion, up 98% year/year and in line with the amount companies raised in the first three quarters of 2021. However, dollar volumes this year have been boosted by a handful of large deals. The number of offerings so far in 2026 indicates less of an issuance boom than a return to normal following four years of muted activity. In Exhibit 29, we evaluate what the market is currently pricing for the regional technology sector in terms of its medium-term ROE and the equity risk premium. Given current 47% ROE and expected 40% earnings CAGR over the next 2 years, the market is pricing a sharp fade in ROE to a 20-26% range equivalent to the 10- to 3-year average levels, depending on cost of equity assumptions. The overarching insight is the longer the AI-driven ROE premium can be sustained at a given cost of equity, the greater the valuation upside for tech, assuming other factors remain unchanged. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley MUFG 9 Potentially Higher Fiscal Costs from Energy Price Support Japan's situation differs from that of some European countries that rely heavily on imported refined petroleum products. Because Japan imports crude oil and refines it domestically into gasoline, diesel, and other petroleum products, upward pressure from supply shortages of refined fuels tends to be more limited as long as crude oil supplies remain secure. In addition, retail fuel prices are currently being further restrained by the government's fuel subsidy program ( Exhibit 11 ). The subsidy scheme consists of a weekly component linked to changes in international benchmark prices and a monthly adjustment factor reflecting refiners' additional procurement costs, including the cost of sourcing alternative supplies. As a result, part of the recent increase in physical crude procurement costs is already being absorbed through fiscal spending. House Where things stand: Prediction markets imply a more than 90% chance that Democrats will net at least the three seats they need to win the House majority. Democrats lead the generic ballot by an average of 8.9pp, implying a roughly 12pp swing from the 2.6pp popular vote margin that House Republicans won with in 2024. Republicans hold seats in 29 districts that President Trump won by less than 12pp, and these are generally the seats that prediction markets and analysts expect to flip (Exhibit 2). Redistricting is likely to net the GOP only a few seats if polling is accurate. The state pension could be adjusted to rise by the higher of inflation or 2.5% in April 2030, while state pension will also hold its value relative to earnings over time. The pension triple lock is an expensive policy. The well-known large trade deficit in goods is offset by a surplus in services and of net income. Trade in services reflects tourism, but also France being competitive in business services. Taken from the distribution of savings within the countries, it offers a very interesting story: the large public deficit, and its widening since 2019, is mirrored by large private savings, which has been increasing since 2019, mostly from households. Ultimately, the issue with France's public deficit is a domestic affair, but the risks that external debt sustainability becomes an issue seems limited. Debt sustainability analysis | Watch r-g: We turn now to debt sustainability analysis (DSA), using the framework we detailed for instance here and here. Fundamentally, we can think about debt dynamic as a function of three parameters: the primary balance as a share of GDP (sp), the apparent interest rate on public debt (r) and nominal GDP growth (g). The key relationship to have in mind is that the primary balance which enables debt to stabilize as a share of GDP (at a level d) is given by sp~d*(r-g). When r-g increases, the primary balance required increases. With current yields on French debt (as observed on average over the past 20 days), r will mechanically rise in the next years. When house prices rise, homeowners feel wealthier and can borrow more against their higher equity. Both encourage more consumption, while falling prices have the opposite effect. Neither make France immune to an interest rate shock, to be clear. They just reduce or delay the direct rates passthrough to the existing stock of loans, though can still lead to a fairly swift impact on lending flows. Our semiconductor analysts expect record n global DRAM and NAND undersupply in 2026 and a further new record shortfall in 2027, with continuing (albeit narrower) undersupply in 2028 extending into 2029-2030 (although our semiconductor analysts do not have formal estimates yet for these outyears). Longest and deepest memory undersupply drives pricing power and n profitability. Customers’ willingness to sign 3- to 5-year long-term agreements (LTAs) and even more stringent strategic customer agreements (SCAs) signals their expectation of tight supply for an extended period, driving sustained favorable pricing for memory manufacturers. Coupled with high operating leverage, this dynamic is delivering unprecedented levels of profitability. Faster supply response unlikely. Assuming continuing rapid demand for compute, n the principal risk to the memory sector’s high level of profitability is a more rapid supply response than is currently forecast. This is unlikely for several reasons. First, supply chain bottlenecks upstream of memory fabs are constraining the elasticity of memory supply. records.text: US Rates Weekly 09 October 2026 Citi Research 8 Short-end: Repo holding steady Repo rates have stayed relatively contained over the past week (Figure 16), in line with our view (see US Rates Weekly - OAT of the blue). We have been arguing that reserves have been in a lightly abundant regime over the past few months, as the increase in T-bill supply from July and August did not pressure repo rates higher (see Figure 17). However, we could see some light upwards pressure in repo rates towards the end of October. First, T-bill settlements, which have now turned positive, should continue growing over the coming weeks (see Figure 18). For example, private T-bill outstanding will increase by around $350bn through the end of November, and we expect it to be over $6.9tn by the end of November. Second, the TGA balance will temporarily be over $1tn during the last week of October, in line with Treasury’s guidance, which in turn will temporarily drain reserves from the system (see Figure 19). T ogether, these two factors could push SOFR fixes lightly above IORB. Figure 16. SOFR has been fixing at or below IORB for more than a month now and we think this can continue for the next couple of weeks. Figure 17. Repo rates did not move significantly higher over the summer amid the increase in T-bill outstanding; however, this could be tested at the end of October when we expect private T-bill outstanding to reach an all-time high ($6.7 4tn). © 2026 Citigroup Inc. Volatility in mobile communication prices has increased noticeably since the introduction of a new methodology in July 2025 (Figure right). 2 The new method captures high -frequency price changes and promotional pricing, with plans entering and exiting the data the main contributors to index variation. The result has been not only greater month -to-month variation, but also a tendency for large m onthly moves to reverse; the 1.1% increase in November 2025 was followed by a 3.3% decline in December, while the 2.2% rise in May this year was followed by a 3.3% decline in June. Over the last year, the market has chased the BoJ’s terminal rate higher with 2y1y as a proxy (Figure 5). If 2y1y was the terminal-rate proxy a year ago and it remains the proxy, we can interpret this as the BoJ simply raising and delaying its arrival at the terminal rate. Hypothetically, if the BoJ were to stop hiking at 1.75%, the market is unlikely to expect a cut to follow because that 1.75% is still lower than its 2% CPI target and only is the midpoint of the BoJ’s neutral rate range. records.text: AI inflationary buildout is behind us; disinflation likely lies ahead Conceptually, AI follows a two-stage inflation cycle: inflationary when you build it, disinflationary when you use it. The inflationary phase is driven by a massive investment boom in data centres, power generation, grid transmission, semiconductors, and related infrastructure. When demand for capital, energy, and skilled labor rises faster than supply can respond, prices move higher. This dynamic is still evident in the US, where power and grid constraints have become key bottlenecks to AI deployment. China, by contrast, has already spent years building out power, transmission networks, industrial capacity, and digital infrastructure. As a result, the most inflationary part of the AI infrastructure-related buildout is likely behind China (see China AI Watch: More growth, less reflation, 8 October 2026). records.text: US Rates Weekly 09 October 2026 Citi Research 17 Similarly in the front-end, convexity adjustments for SOFR Blues (Figure 36) and Golds packs currently look low relative to their model fair values, which are strongly tied to front-end implied rates vols. Essentially this means that investors who are looking to be long front-end vol can find better risk/reward by being long SOFR futures convexity adjustments. As a reminder, convexity adjustments represent the differences in rates between the SOFR futures and the maturity-matched Forward Rate Agreements (FRA). The higher rate in the SFR contract (which has no convexity) can be viewed as the compensation for the positive convexity benefit that is found in the corresponding FRA (from a long position’s perspective). The trade-off between SFR’s convexity- adjusted favorable rate and the FRA’s positively convex profile is analogous to the trade-off between the upfront premium and the long gamma profile of an option. In both instances, the PnLs when held to maturity are dependent on the magnitude of the realized rate moves relative to the initial expected breakevens. Large rate moves in volatile markets would help the long convexity/long gamma positions in overcoming the breakevens that are represented by the convexity adjustments/option premiums. records.text: IMPORTANT EQUITY RESEARCH DISCLOSURES, PLEASE SEE PAGE 30. FOR IMPORTANT FIXED INCOME RESEARCH DISCLOSURES, PLEASE SEE PAGE 31. AI in China From AI investment to adoption China's AI push is shifting from ambition to execution. Investment support, and limited infrastructure and regulatory constraints, as well as early signals of adoption, are driving varied economic effects on growth, FX and credit. What China aims to achieve: China's AI strategy reflects a national drive for technological leadership, with policymakers targeting AI adoption across more than 100 industries and a 90% penetration rate by 2030. The strategy is supported by open-model economics and a rapid buildout of public and private AI infrastructure. While macro evidence remains fragmented, we see signs of AI adoption, led by manufacturing and ICT , especially among larger corporates. Sustainability: no major constraints: Sustainability-related factors are set to support, not constrain, China's AI expansion. Adequate power, fuel supply, permitting and spare capacity should enable further AI infrastructure expansion, while water stress remains a localized issue. On adoption, policy priorities are shifting toward workforce reskilling and AI content governance. By contrast, our thematic analysis of the US suggests a shift from AI experimentation toward execution and ROI, alongside a convergence of supply-side constraints (eg, power, labor, permitting, and local opposition). If a delay can be attributed to parliament, i.e. if parliament fails to reach a decision, Art. 47(3) allows the government to bring the provisions into force by a "budget ordinance", which is adopted by the Council of Ministers and does not require parliamentary ratification (unlike the usual procedure in Art. 38, whereby ordinances require parliamentary approval). If instead the delay is caused by the government, i.e. if a budget bill is not presented to parliament in time for promulgation by the end of the year, or if parliament rejects a budget draft within the 70-day period and leaves too little time for the government to present an alternative draft, the provisions of Art. 47(4) and Art 45 of the organic law apply. These allow the government to: (1) Ask parliament before 11 December to adopt the first part of the budget bill (dealing with revenues) first, and the second part (dealing with expenditures) at a later stage; or (2) Request parliamentary authorisation before 19 December for a special law to collect existing taxes and – once the special law has been passed – adopt decrees to implement the appropriations established in last year's budget, essentially ensuring budget continuity. It is this decline in the saving rate that is worth explor- ing to better understand how households have used their bal- ance sheet to cushion spending. Debt rise drives saving rate decline The FAD show that the drop in the personal saving rate since 2023 does not reflect a slowing in the pace of asset accumula- tion but rather a rise in the pace of liability accumulation (Figure 4). As a share of DPI, the net acquisition of financial assets has risen slightly by 0.4%-point. All else equal, this should have lifted the saving rate. But this has been tempered by a modest move lower in the pace of tangible asset accumulation. On net, the pace of overall asset accumulation has not changed much since late-2023. By contrast, the pace of increase in lia- bilities has jumped nearly 2%-points over the past 2.5 years, reducing the saving rate by the same magnitude. The surge in AI-related exports has been largely a price and value-added story rather than a volume story, and these industries are far more capital-intensive than labor-intensive. Moreover, Chinese firms are adopting AI, robotics, and automation primarily to improve efficiency, and reduce labor intensity. AI enables factories to produce more with fewer workers, particularly in routine assembly, quality control, logistics, and administrative functions. As a result, the number of manufacturing workers in China in 2025 was roughly 30% below its 2013 peak. In other words, AI is boosting productivity and output, but not generating enough new jobs to offset the broader decline in manufacturing employment. • Services. The same is true in services. Most corporate AI adoption is concentrated in customer service, back-office operations, coding assistance, financial processing, marketing, and document review, where the primary goal is to automate routine tasks and reduce headcount, not expand payrolls. While AI is creating some high-skilled jobs in software engineering, data science, model development, and cloud infrastructure, the numbers are too small to offset broader weakness in white-collar hiring. It is likely that the OBR will increase its forecast for wage growth later this month to reflect higher-than-expected inflation, but to what extent is uncertain. In contrast, the Bank of England has consistently forecast higher wage growth than the OBR in the medium term. In its latest forecasts, the Bank forecasts wage growth of 3.1% on average each year from 2026 to 2028 relative to 2.8% in our forecasts. These differences in forecast nominal wage growth are due to a combination of different views on different factors including: the path for inflation; the extent to which an inflation shock passes through to wages; medium- run productivity growth; and the share of future productivity gains that workers receive. For instance, the Bank of England estimates assume firms’ profit margins do not add to inflation in the medium term, leaving more space for wages to expand without pushing up inflation. While this may be true in the medium term, we think in the near term the rebuilding of margins against a backdrop of weak demand is likely to weigh against wage growth. records.text: How Does China’s Petchem Market Work? China’s petchem market is complex, featuring interwoven supply chains along which many different key intermediates (“building blocks”) and end-use chemicals are produced from the same feedstocks. We focus on the supply chains of three major “building blocks” for which we have plant-level data and which involve switching pathways: ethylene, propylene, and monoethylene glycol (MEG)1 (Exhibit 4). Ethylene and propylene are direct derivatives of oil or coal2 and serve as precursors n for over 60% of commercial end-use chemicals; they can be co-produced or produced separately, depending on the process3. MEG is a downstream derivative of ethylene that can also be produced directly from n coal. A single plant that is designed to use oil (in the case of ethylene/propylene) or ethylene (in the case of MEG) as a feedstock cannot simply switch to using coal, and vice versa. Rather, “switching” occurs in aggregate as individual plants optimize how hard they run based on feedstock-specific margins—if oil becomes more expensive than coal, then oil-based ethylene margins drop below coal-based ones, oil-based plants run less hard, and aggregate consumption of oil declines relative to that of coal4. Both extend voyage times, reducing the number of trips each tanker can complete. The arithmetic is straightforward: the longer each vessel spends moving cargo, the more vessels are needed to transport the same amount of oil. Sanctions add another layer of complexity. Around 124 Iranian VLCCs, equivalent to roughly 13% of the global fleet, remain effectively unavailable to much of the international market because of US sanctions. Many are anchored or drifting in the Gulf or offshore locations near Sri Lanka and Malaysia, their physical presence offering little relief to the mainstream tanker market. The result is a sharp increase in the number of vessels required to move essentially the same amount of crude. Compared with the 2025 average, transporting Middle Eastern crude (excluding Iran) now requires an additional 35 VLCCs, 13 Suezmaxes, and 10 Aframaxes (Tables 1-3). As the Middle East absorbs a growing share of the available fleet, other regions are left competing for increasingly scarce transportation capacity. In the rest of the world, for example, VLCC employment has fallen by 16 vessels. Atlantic Basin producers are responding by moving crude on smaller vessels. A single VLCC cargo can be replaced by roughly two Suezmaxes or three Aframaxes, spreading the shortage across the tanker market (Table 4). O

That means delivering a projected budget surplus (Stability Rule) and reducing Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities (PSNFL) as a share of GDP (Investment Rule) by 2029/30. However, we think it’s possible that the Chancellor may positively surprise markets with a fiscal headroom that is slightly larger than this. Second is the promise of “breathing space” to UK households and firms consistent with Labour’s cost-of-living pledge. We expect some initiatives in this Budget that aim to provide short-term relief to some households and businesses. For households, these policies will likely be means-tested (or only for those already on benefits), while for businesses, we expect the policies to target SMEs. These short-term policies will likely be oversold politically, with heavy briefing from the Treasury about them, while at the same time being limited in scale to avoid eating too far into the fiscal headroom. A brief history of quantitative easing and quantitative tightening Quantitative easing (QE) was rolled out in 2009 during the financial crisis to help stimulate the economy out of recession and bring inflation up to the Bank of England’s 2% target. It was an untested tool and there was limited precedent to inform its design. In order to let the Bank of England focus on its aim of stabilising the economy, rather than concerns of the potential profit and loss inherent in holding a large portfolio, the Bank and the government agreed that the bonds purchased would be held in a legally separate entity rather than directly on the balance sheet of the Bank of England. This entity was termed the Asset Purchase Facility (APF). The government then guaranteed, or indemnified, the financial position of this facility, meaning HM Treasury would make good on any losses that were incurred. eaway? The PBoC is likely to tolerate further gradual CNY appreciation, but has limited tolerance for a rapid or large move. China’s exports have become less sensitive to exchange-rate movements as the export mix has shifted towards higher-tech, higher-margin products, giving policymakers greater scope to accommodate gradual currency strength. However, the impact of appreciation would remain uneven. Labour-intensive, low-margin exporters remain more exposed, and rapid appreciation could intensify pressure on these sectors and the labour market. This should keep the PBoC focused on managing the pace of appreciation rather than opposing CNY strength outright. A stronger floor, but also a lower ceiling This translates into a stronger floor under CNY , but also a lower ceiling on the speed of appreciation. The PBoC’s rejection of competitive depreciation signals low tolerance for disorderly weakness. However, concerns about domestic demand, employment and export competitiveness argue against interpreting the statement as an invitation to push USDCNY sharply lower. This creates a meaningful policy asymmetry. The PBoC remains more concerned about disorderly depreciation because of its implications for capital outflows, confidence and financial stability. Household resilience built over the boom Household balance sheets remain resilient despite the cash rate rising 100bp in 2026 to 4.6%, a 15-year high. According to the RBA, fewer than 2% of variable-rate owner- occupier borrowers are currently experiencing a cash flow shortfall. This strength reflects years of house price gains, moderate growth in liabilities, and a still-tight labour market supporting incomes, although the recent housing downturn is likely to gradually erode some of these wealth gains. Liquidity buffers for a rainy day The key buffer behind this resilience is liquidity. The median mortgage borrower holds offset and redraw balances sufficient to cover more than a year of scheduled repayments at current interest rates, a stronger position than before the pandemic. This resilience is broad-based, with the median mortgage prepayment buffer larger than pre- pandemic levels across all income quartiles. While this strength is broad-based, borrowers with high loan-to-value and loan-to-income ratios continue to show higher arrears than the broader market. Bank of Canada Implications We continue to expect the Bank of Canada to remain on hold at 2.25% through 2026 and 2027. In September, the Bank turned more hawkish, dropping its assessment that policy "remains appropriate" and flagging higher upside risks to inflation from persistent energy prices, and we had highlighted December as the first meeting at which a hike could become plausible. That required, among other conditions, domestic activity remaining resilient as the expected consumption slowdown takes hold. Two months of softer employment, a higher unemployment rate, a lower job-finding rate, and contained wage growth move the labor market in the other direction, lowering the likelihood that those conditions line up by October or December. Nor does the print revive a case for cuts. The weakness is concentrated in the public sector and in education, where it reflects fiscal restraint and immigration policy rather than the cyclical demand the Bank can influence. Private-sector employment is stable, layoffs are low, payroll growth through the summer was positive, and the falling participation rate is primarily demographic. The October MPR will be the Bank's first full reassessment since the hawkish shift, incorporating the September CPI and labor data. Page 2 When Warsh last spoke at the September FOMC meeting, he outlined a relatively hawkish case for the policy outlook, namely that policy is currently accommodative and they took the first move to “remove a dose of accommodation”. But the minutes to that meeti ng revealed a variety of motivations for hiking: “many” officials focused on risk management or “insurance” considerations; “a number” thought tighter policy was needed to combat higher inflation in their modal outlooks; “some” wanted to tighten to prevent inflation expectations unanchoring; “a couple” wanted to prevent second round or spillover effects from supply shocks or raised their neutral rate estimates. Finally, “several…viewed the current policy rate as not restrictive or only mildly restrictive”, a view Warsh indicated had become broadly accepted in the Committee. Outside of Warsh, we will look for Fedspeak this week to reveal which officials fall into these camps. In short, barring a meaningful (and broad-based) upside miss on this week’s inflation data, we expect the Fed to remain on hold at the October meeting in order to gat her more information on underlying trends (see “ US Economic Perspectives: Trend inflation edges lower, tightening bias endures“) as well as monitor financial conditions in the wake of sharp moves in global interest rates (see “US Economic Chartbook: Monthly charts: How high to tighten FCIs?“). Disinflationary fiscal measures such as extension to VAT cuts and the fuel duty freeze, along with further policy costs off energy bills can lower inflation by 20bps in 2027. The BoE will be encouraged by the disinflationary measures. But we think the Budget is unlikely to be material enough to affect our call of two hikes in November and February unless the measures are larger than we expect (though it may reduce market pricing of close to four hikes). Even considering these measures, inflation could peak at close to 4% in early 2027, a level at which we think the BoE would get worried about risks of second round effects, if the energy shock is prolonged. The profile of energy prices and evidence on risks of second round effects are a more material input to our call. Bigger challenges for later Overall, we expect a relatively cautious and low-key budget, focussing on stability and the devolution agenda. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 France 2026 vs Italy 2022 In this box, we compare France in 2026 to Italy in 2022, from a debt sustainability perspective 1 Our main conclusion is that France's public finances today do not look necessarily more sustainable than Italy's public finances did in 2022. The ability of Italy to post primary surpluses is of course key. Higher Italian debt and a sharp reduction of the deficit in 2024: The first and well-known fact is that public debt in Italy is higher than in France (Exhibit 14). It stood at 138% of GDP in 2022 while France is at 115% in 2025 (moving close to 120% in 2026). Turning to deficits, France's deficit was 5.1% of GDP in 2025 (Exhibit 15 ) and we think it will be at 5.4% in 2026. Public deficit was even larger in 2022 in Italy (8.1% of GDP) as it was strongly affected by the Superbonus (a tax credit for households renovating their homes) and energy-related measures. Italy's deficit has rapidly corrected since, getting close to 3% in 2024. This rapid correction in 2024 deserves further investigation. From an accounting perspective, it reflects to a significant degree the termination of the Superbonus. But this correction should also probably not be viewed independently from the 2022 financial tensions. As we will detail below, it was in any case key to put Italian debt on a broadly stable trajectory. records.text: 1 “Internet+ and Artificial Intelligence Three-Year Action and Implementation Plan“, National Development and Reform Commission, Ministry of Science and Technology, Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, Cyberspace Administration of China, May 2016 Macroeconomics: AI’s macro impact comes in several channels at different horizons. While the near-term contribution is likely to be led by exports and AI infrastructure capex, we think the longer-term contribution to growth will come through higher total factor productivity, as firms use AI to improve efficiency across manufacturing and services. Our other observations are that the most inflationary phase of China's AI-related infrastructure buildout is likely behind us and AI has yet to create enough jobs, with demand insufficient to counter the property downturn and automation. FX & rates: Given the limited near-term growth impact of AI-driven productivity, we see FX and rates being driven more by the AI export cycle than by productivity gains from AI adoption. China’s AI boom is more supportive of the CNY than it is bearish for CGBs. For rates, AI should keep the PBoC accommodative and CGB yields relatively low. The stronger growth impulse is more relevant for CNY NDIRS, where it reduces easing expectations and leaves the 5y sector more exposed than the policy-anchored front end. There is no simple definition of a bond crisis. US Supreme Court Justice Potter Stewart’s famous turn of phrase with regards to a threshold test for obscenity (‘I know it when I see it’) could easily be applied to bond market crises. A 21st century bond crisis is not necessarily characterised by uncovered auctions (auctions with insufficient demand at acceptable prices to the issuer), spiralling yields and a triumph of the ‘bond vigilantes’ . Rather, if the experience of the UK in 2022 is anything to go by, it can be a more technically complex story about credibility, leverage and market structure. Crises frequently start slowly until a trigger acts as an accelerant on a transmission mechanism, requiring rapid corrective policy interventions. That trigger can be a loss of confidence in fiscal policymaking and institutional processes, or simply a liquidity event that begins a chain reaction, with leverage acting as a financial accelerant. In 2022, a key problem was the degree of hidden leverage embedded in UK LDI strategies. This leverage was the transmission mechanism, which turned a sharp sell-off following Chancellor Kwarteng’s mini-Budget into a much wider crisis. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 Financial Conditions: Restrictive, but not unusually so How restrictive is monetary policy? At the September FOMC meeting, Chair Warsh said the Fed removed “a dose of accommodation.” Are financial conditions accommodative? We take a fresh look at the stance of policy and financial conditions and conclude that financial conditions are modestly restrictive; more of a headwind than a brake. The Fed raised the federal funds rate by 25bp to 3.75–4.00% in September, citing resilient domestic spending, robust AI-related business spending and above-target inflation. Yet Chair Warsh questioned the usefulness of treating an estimated neutral interest rate as an operational guide to policy, arguing that credit markets showed few signs of policy restraint. We approach the question—is monetary policy restrictive?—from two directions. First, we estimate the neutral policy rate using a New Keynesian framework, asking what real short rate is consistent with the observed configuration of the output gap, unemployment gap and inflation gap. Second, we examine the stance of broader financial conditions and the channels through which the policy rate is (or is not) restraining private demand. On net, our two-track approach suggests that monetary policy is neutral to modestly restrictive while financial conditions are restrictive, but not unusually so. Risk Premium Reflects Market Fears of Oil Supply Disruption The near-record risk premium reflects both investors’ and physical crude buyers’ fears of potential geopolitical escalation in the Middle East that would further disrupt oil exports and damage oil infrastructure. In fact, we show that the risk premium moves closely with proxies for oil supply disruption risk, including Brent call option implied volatility skew (which reflects financial demand for options-based protection against price spikes) and the news-based geopolitical risk index (Exhibit 8). Speculative Investing and Macro Portfolio Hedging Financial demand for paper barrels has been also driving prices higher this year (Exhibit 9, left panel). We find that the risk premium has been moving closely with active investor oil positioning over the last several years, whether driven by direct profit-seeking amid large oil price moves or by portfolio hedging (Exhibit 9, right panel).3 3 Speculative investor positioning is difficult to predict but has a historical tendency to revert to the mean. The yield curve spread described above can be directly measured: it is simply the difference between yields on long- and short-term bonds. But a steeper curve can be indicative of a higher (or unstable) term premium and this must be estimated. Specifically, the term premium is an inferred measure of how much of the long-term yield reflects compensation for bearing the additional uncertainty associated with holding a longer-term bond (instead of a series of short- term bonds). Typically, the term premium is interpreted as a bigger driver of moves in longer- maturity issues (10 years and longer) than moves in shorter-maturity issues, where changing policy rate expectations are likely more important. Figure 10 shows the model-estimated 10-year term premium for the US, Germany and UK. The UK term premium – while elevated – has not materially increased in the last year. This suggests the move in yields on long-term gilts over the last year was mainly driven by evolving central bank policy rate expectations, rather than by moves in the term premium component of yields. Equity buffers still ample, but thinning as house prices fall Home equity provides the second line of defence. Dwelling prices have risen 62% over the past decade, which included 4 downturns. There were two elements to his proposal: the first is a pledge to find funding for £4.7 billion in this Budget 2; and the second is to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035. The latter commitment has been delayed, but the Chancellor needs to find £4.7 billion. T o complicate matters, the new Labour government also announced an £8.4 billion investment on their Dreadnought Programme, via the Defence Nuclear Enterprise. We think the most likely scenario is for this programme to be swallowed as part of the wider Defence Investment Plan, and for the £4.7 billion to be repurposed into funding the Dreadnought Programme (at least partially). Either way, most of the defence spending initiatives are likely to be captured in the umbrella of the PSNFL (Investment Rule), and so the net gain on its net financial liabilities will be neutral, as it borrows from the liabilities side of its balance sheet against the defence assets it is building on the other side. However, this budget will hold off on solving the big questions. This is perhaps a sensible strategy for the time-being as the public have both little tolerance for pension and welfare cuts, on the one hand, and further tax rises or breaking manifesto pledges on the other. LLC Arunima Sinha Global Economist Arunima.Sinha@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-4125 September Employment - Cooling From a Hot Summer Bottom Line: Canada shed 68k jobs in September (Prior: -42k), a second consecutive decline that brings the two-month give-back to 110k and unwinds most of the 181k gained from April to July. We had expected a moderation after an unusually strong summer: employment is still up 71k since April and 95k (+0.5%) from a year ago, and the payroll survey (SEPH), albeit lagged, continues to point to a firmer underlying trend than the LFS now suggests. The composition supports that read. The losses were concentrated in the public sector, educational services and youth, while private-sector employment was little changed and layoffs remain low. The unemployment rate rose only 0.1pp to 6.5%, cushioned by a fall in participation to 64.8% that is largely the product of population aging rather than discouraged workers. Section 338 and other tariff uncertainty is not impacting manufacturing employment, which remains essentially flat on the year as businesses adapt– consistent with the BoC's views. We read the print as consistent with our call for the Bank of Canada to remain on hold at 2.25% through 2026 and 2027: it takes some heat out of the hawkish tilt from September without reopening a case for cuts. We have added to the traditional quadrant approach using regime clusters based on cross-correlations of macro-economic variables. We transitioned back to normal or expansionary part of the cycle from the more risky-asset- challenged “Tightening of Financial Conditions” cluster in the aftermath of last April’s “Liberation Day” tariff announcements. After a brief “Goldilocks” moment, we moved back to the “Normal” cluster in April, and we remain there today. Our nearest-neighbor model is highlighting we appear later in the cycle however. records.text: was not the primary aim of the policy. Instead, the QE programme aimed to stimulate growth, at a time when the UK economy was in recession. Higher growth would also have been positive for the government’s finances. Viewed narrowly, QT acts in reverse on both these channels. However, the difference for QT is that, with interest rates still a long way from the low levels of the 2010s, the Bank can, and does, look to offset this drag by setting Bank Rate lower than it might otherwise have done, meaning the macroeconomic costs of QT through this channel are likely to be less than the benefits of QE. Any broader evaluation of the fiscal consequences of the programme should take these indirect channels into account. How big are these financial flows, and what has changed recently? Scale of financial flows Between 2009 and 2022, the APF was making a profit and the cumulative cash flows to HM Treasury peaked at £123.9 billion in Q3 2022.1 Since then, money has flowed back the other way at an average pace of around £30 billion per year. By the end of Q2 2026 the net cumulative flows to the Treasury remained positive, but just, at £16.2 billion: HM Treasury has roughly broken even on the QE/QT programme so far. Continuing losses mean this is likely to turn to a cumulative loss by early next year. 11 October 2026 4 Barclays | UK Themes

Looking forward, we expect $600 billion of primary corporate equity issuance in 2027. The macro backdrop should support continued issuance in 2027 as economic growth remains solid and interest rates retreat from current levels. On the other side of the ledger, we expect corporate equity demand via buybacks and cash M&A will exceed $2 trillion. Including expiring lockups, net US public equity supply will likely increase next year by the largest amount since 2000. However, it is unrealistic to assume that all unlocked shares will be immediately sold. In addition, we expect that much of the liquid wealth created by the sale of unlocked shares will eventually result in additional equity demand. We exclude equity issuance via stock-based compensation from our analysis. We do not expect additional equity supply to derail the bull market in the near future. The shifting balance between corporate equity supply and demand adds to the various macro and micro factors pressuring equity valuations. However, Federal Reserve data show US household equity purchases exceeding $800 billion in H1 2026, with non-US investors adding more than $350 billion in additional demand. Our outlook for continued earnings growth alongside declining yields should support continued investor demand for equities. records.text: The decline in China oil end-use demand has played a key role in reducing the n global oil deficit and upward crude price pressure due to the Hormuz shock. While gasoline and diesel demand is likely to remain low as long as China product prices remain high, we see the decline in oil demand from the petrochemicals (“petchem”) sector as much less sustainable for two reasons. First, nearly one-third of the Q2 weakness in China demand for oil products used n in the petchem sector reversed by August. Second, while fuel switching (including the growing usage of electric vehicles) has n driven much of the weakness in China gasoline and diesel end-use demand, we estimate only a modest contribution from feedstock switching to the weakness in China petchem oil demand. Using plant-level capacity and utilization data, we estimate that oil-to-coal n switching explains only 19% of the Q2 hit to China petchem oil demand, and naphtha-to-ethane switching explains just 8%. The vast majority of the decline (73%) was due to lower production of petchem products, which likely largely reflected downstream destocking (and is not sustainable in the long-term) and potentially also some price-induced end-use demand destruction. records.text: ugh house price drawdown (%) vs dwelling index (RHS) Source: Cotality BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH Wealth effects should weigh on consumption We estimate a 10% fall in house prices lowers consumption by around 1.3% in the long run, with much of the effect coming through within the first year. Our estimates are broadly similar to RBA1 analysis which estimated that around half of the consumption response occurs within the two quarters of a housing wealth shock. When house prices rise, homeowners feel wealthier and can borrow more against their higher equity. Both encourage more consumption, while falling prices have the opposite effect. Lower housing activity flow through the GDP Falling house prices rarely occur in isolation. The current decline is coinciding with a gradual easing in the labour market, and a weaker housing market would add to the broader slowdown through lower consumption, dwelling investment and business investment. While the RBA’s focus is currently on elevated inflation, we expect the continued fall in house prices will be a key factor leading to an RBA pivot in 2027. A housing downturn is likely to weigh on the economy through multiple channels beyond consumption.
