Reflation camp's response to a December rate hike will be in focus This week, a series of remarks from government and BoJ officials signaled a departure from the traditional reflationist stance. Prime Minister Takaichi stated that “this is not a phase that requires reflationary policies,” while BoJ board member Sato, widely viewed as a reflationist, endorsed gradual rate hikes despite characterizing financial conditions as still accommodative. The key question for the December meeting, where a rate hike is expected, is whether this shift will be reflected in voting behavior. If Sato switches to supporting a rate hike, the policy significance would be substantial. Looking ahead, a more centrist composition following the July policy board appointments next year could lead the BoJ to proceed with rate hikes at a more gradual pace. That said, there is no major change to our terminal rate view. We estimate Japan’s neutral rate at around 2%, and see policy rates exceeding our 2% forecast only in scenarios involving a stronger acceleration in wages and inflation or the BoJ falling behind the curve on the exchange rate. Will long-term interest rates rise further? Japan’s 10-year government bond yield has reached 3.1%, its highest level in roughly 30 years. records.text: 6 Global Economic Weekly | 09 October 2026 If this isn’t forward guidance, what is? We were also baffled by the heavy-handedness of last week’s Fed communication. Williams and Jefferson pushed back against an Oct hike even before seeing the Sep data. If Warsh was on board with their communication, his strong stated objection to forward guidance isn’t credible. If he wasn’t on board, he is at risk of ceding the bully pulpit. Either way, it’s a problematic situation. What would an Oct pause mean for the Fed outlook? If the Fed pauses in Oct, we think the most likely policy path would be two more 25bp hikes, in Dec 2026 and Mar 2027. However, the risks to that outlook would be two sided. On the one hand, by moving slower the Fed might end up having to do more. So we wouldn’t rule out additional hikes in Jun and perhaps even Sep 2027. On the other hand, if y/y core inflation were to roll off due to favorable base effects next year, the Fed might stop after just one more hike in Dec 2026. In this scenario, the Fed’s caution would be vindicated. We think markets might even test the Fed’s resolve to hike in Dec. At the moment they are pricing just about one full hike by Dec. But pricing could come off meaningfully if we get soft jobs or inflation data and the Fed doesn’t clearly guide markets toward a hike. We’re sticking with our call for a hike in Oct for now, but we’ll re-assess next week after the September inflation data and Chair Warsh’s comments at the IMF meetings on Thursda

records.text: Our Brent Price Framework We model Brent spot prices as the sum of long-dated prices and timespreads, defined as spot prices (nearby Brent futures) minus long-dated prices (36-month-ahead Brent futures) (Exhibit 1). We model WTI spot prices as Brent spot prices plus a WTI-Brent differential, which depends on factors such as tanker freight costs. Long-dated Brent is a slower-moving price anchor that is typically pinned down by marginal costs of oil production, effective production spare capacity, and market expectations of long-run oil demand. Our long-dated Brent 3-year ahead fair value estimate remains $76.2 The Brent 1M/36M timespread — the more dynamic component of our price framework — can be further decomposed into an inventory-based fair value, an interest rate e ffect, and a residual timespread risk premium. High interest rates lower timespreads—the value of owning oil today relative to the value of oil in the future—by increasing the opportunity cost of holding oil. Arbitrage opportunities between futures and spot markets imply a one-for-one negative relationship between rates and timespreads, and our framework incorporates a 3pp decline in the Brent 1M/36M timespread per 1pp increase in the 3-year Treasury yield (or a 3pp increase in the cumulative yield over 3 years). In this Oil Analyst, we zoom in on the two remaining components of our framework — the stock-based fair value of the timespread and the timespread risk premium. We estimate that China's AI-related investment will likely reach CNY960bn in 2026 and hit CNY1.25tn in 2027 (Figure 33), reflecting rising spending by hyperscalers, telecom operators and data-centre developers. AI is generating new investments spanning data centres, cloud infrastructure, semiconductors, networking equipment and power systems. However, the macro impact of AI investment remains modest. We estimate that AI-related investment accounts for less than 2% of China's total investment, making it too small to fully offset the drag from property and slower infrastructure spending (these two combined accounted for 67% of total investment). After adjusting for imported chips and equipment, and land that do not directly add to current real GDP , we estimate AI-related investment could contribute roughly 0.3ppt to annual GDP growth in 2026 followed by 0.2pp in 2027. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 09 October 2026 5 Slow and steady One argument in favor of quarterly hikes is that although the Fed is facing only a moderate overshoot in underlying inflation, it has little sense of how far it will have to go to get inflation back to target. Sequential hikes could lead markets to price in too aggressive a policy path, as they probably did until last week. And pausing after a few hikes might convey a false sense of confidence that the Fed has done enough to get inflation back to target. By hiking slowly but steadily, the Fed would give itself more time to assess the data and determine the appropriate terminal rate. This is a reasonable argument, though we’d note that no policymaker has articulated it clearly. Waller probably came the closest. Williams and Jefferson’s calls for patience were much more one-sided: they argued against another move in Oct but did not acknowledge the risk that the Fed might have to hike significantly further. Spooked by the bond The Fed also appears to be spooked by the spike in long-end rates. Jefferson was explicit about this. It makes sense for the Fed to lean against disorderly market moves. But it isn’t clear to us whether hiking or holding is better for the long end. Markets might view a decisive Fed as more credible on inflation than a hesitant one. records.text: Near Record Risk Premium We estimate the risk premium as the difference between the realized Brent 1M/36M timespread and the fair value predicted by our stock-based model. Our updated model implies an average risk premium of $22/bbl in September—the second highest monthly reading on record after April 2026 (Exhibit 6). Focusing only on OECD commercial stocks would imply a higher risk premium estimate of $29/bbl, but this approach wouldn’t capture the physical market tightness outside of the OECD. The estimated September risk premium is very high relative to its historical distribution (excluding 2020) (Exhibit 7). For instance, the peak monthly risk premium estimate during the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022 did not exceed $16/bbl, highlighting how unprecedented this year’s oil supply shock has been. Although we assume the risk premium gradually returns to its historical average of zero, in line with its typical statistical pattern of mean reversion, it may remain elevated even as continued adaptation eases physical tightness. We plan to refine this point in our framework in a detailed balance update soon. UK Themes The direct fiscal effects of quantitative easing and tightening HM Treasury is currently making annual payments to cover the Asset Purchase Facility’s losses as the Bank of England’s programme of quantitative easing is unwound. This chapter summarises how the APF works and how flows between the APF and HM Treasury impact the public finances. Key findings 1. Since 2009, the Bank of England has bought significant quantities of government1. bonds, and some corporate bonds, through its quantitative easing (QE) programme. These are held in the Asset Purchase Facility (APF), a legally separate entity which is indemnified by HM Treasury. Between 2009 and 2022, the APF was making a profit and a policy choice was made to send these immediately to HM Treasury. These had amounted to £124 billion in total by Q3 2022. 2. Following the annual GDP revisions and a mark-to-market update, we forecast growth of 2.6% 4Q/4Q 2026. For 2027, we continue to forecast trend-like 2.1% 4Q/4Q growth. Tailwinds from AI investment, a positive wealth effect and improving job growth support our view that the economy will remain strong despite headwinds from energy prices and a small fiscal drag next year. Inflation: Underlying inflation stuck above target • Downward revisions to core PCE inflation came in slightly larger than we anticipated. We now see 4Q/4Q core PCE inflation at 3.1% in 2026 and expect it to remain above 2% all through 2027. While revisions lowered our near-term inflation outlook, we still see underlying inflation running near 2.5%, with little progress over the past year. We view the risks to inflation as skewed to the upside, including strong AI-related investment, labor supply constraints from lower migration and aging demographics, trade policy uncertainty, the Iran war, and robust consumer demand. Labor market: Roughly in balance • We have made mark-to-market changes to our labor outlook. We expect job growth to average 70k/mo in '26, comfortably above breakeven. Today, with regional flows largely restored, the pressure is coming increasingly from transportation rather than the underlying availability of oil. In April, the market was paying a premium for scarce barrels. Today, it is paying a premium to move them. There is, however, a limit to how high freight rates can rise. That limit is ultimately determined by refining economics. Refiners can absorb higher transportation costs only as long as the margins earned from converting crude into refined products justify the expense. Record-high product cracks have so far provided an unusually large cushion, allowing tanker freight rates to climb to levels that would previously have seemed difficult to sustain. But that cushion is not unlimited. If refining margins weaken, charterers’ willingness to pay for transportation could fall sharply, even when vessel availability remains tight. There are signs that this threshold may have been reached this week. records.text: Valuation: Separating tech from non-tech The information technology sector is now the dominant contributor to regional earnings following exceptional growth and profitability. This raises questions of how to value tech, whether the market has overpaid for the earnings boom, and what the appropriate methodology for assessing regional valuation should be. Similar to our approach to earnings, we find a strong case for assessing tech and non-tech valuations separately and then combining them to arrive at a composite regional view. We use a DDM approach to value tech as this takes current super-normal profits into explicit account and apply our top-down macro modeling to the non-tech part of the region. The bottom line is we find the market is underpricing both tech and non-tech and estimate 16% valuation upside for hard tech, 3% for non-tech, and 10% for the MXAPJ regional index as whole (from 10.3x to 11.3x on a 12m forward basis). Has the market overpaid for strong tech earnings? As an initial check on whether market performance has exceeded tech sector profit delivery, we find that market capitalization of the regional tech hardware & semiconductor sector has moved roughly in line with delivered earnings. On this metric, recent strong tech share price performance reflects underlying profit growth rather than undue optimism over AI. PM Meloni’s government has been the most long-lived in Italian post WWII history. Italy is now scheduled to hold its general election in 2027, most likely in April or September. The tight political competition between the ruling coalition and the opposition has already raised demands for more fiscal support. In our view, there are two key elements to watch in the next election: whether the election delivers a clear parliamentary majority that could extend political stability for another 5 years, and whether the next majority raises fiscal slippage risk. The ruling majority proposed an electoral reform that would replace the current hybrid system, 1/3 first-past-the-post and 2/3 proportional representation, with full proportional representation corrected by a majority premium for the winning coalition if it reaches at least 42% of the votes in both chambers. The final vote on the reform is planned for 8 October, and we expect the Parliament to approve it. Under the new system, broad coalition-building will be rewarded with a clear majority, making the fiscal stance of the winning bloc key for market participants. Opinion polls point to a small gap between centre-right and centre-left coalitions, with coalition expansion likely to determine whether either side gains a decisive edge. records.text: Japan Macro Watch 9 October 2026 ab 2 Reflation camp's response to a December rate hike in focus This week saw a series of remarks from policymakers that could be interpreted as a coordinated rejection of reflationary policy. Following Minister Kiuchi, Prime Minister Takaichi stated during Thursday’s plenary session of the House of Representatives that “the current situation does not call for reflationary policies,” while also emphasizing that the government fully respects the Bank of Japan’s independence. In addition, former BoJ Deputy Governor Wakatabe, who serves as a private-sector member of the Council on Economic and Fiscal Policy, made comments rejecting reflation-style policies. Similar remarks were also heard from BoJ Policy Board member Sato, who has generally been viewed as part of the reflation camp. In exclusive interviews with Kyodo News and Asahi Shimbun on Wednesday, Sato acknowledged that risks such as weak private consumption remain. At the same time, he argued that financial conditions remain accommodative and expressed support for a gradual increase in the policy rate. Taken together, this week’s comments suggest that the policy stance of the reflation camp may be shifting more significantly than we had previously assumed. At the December Monetary Policy Meeting, where a majority of market participants expect a rate hike, attention will focus on whether this change in rhetoric translates into actual voting behaviour. records.text: and Throughout the Hiking Cycle Going into, and throughout the early stages of the hiking cycles, curves tend to trade with a strong flattening bias, with 2s10s flattening on average 30bp in the 100 days around the first hike. That said, that flattening pattern is much more pronounced in the 2s5s curve segment, with less follow-through in 5s10s or 10s30s (Exhibit 7). This has made the post-hike steepening observed in the current cycle stand out (Exhibit 6). While fundamental factors have likely contributed, we think this mainly reflects risk premium given the volatile market conditions throughout September and tepid demand in selloffs, despite attractive valuations. In turn, once hikes have concluded and focus shifts to future easing, the back end of the curve typically steepens more, while the front end to belly rallies broadly in parallel. In other words, going into hikes the belly typically outperforms more than it underperforms going out of hikes (Exhibit 7). This pattern is even more pronounced in the US than for its peers. Given the belly underperformance so far and significant hike premium versus our baseline, we think the 5-10y part of the curve offers the most value for longs. This is because of a judgmental assessment in the way the BEA defines saving in the NIPA. Margin lending on financial assets is not included in liabilities from a personal saving flow perspective because this type of debt is viewed as a pure financial asset swap. Notably, this contrasts with real estate loans (e.g. mortgages, including home equity lines of credit), which reflect a physical underlying asset that the BEA choos- es to treat differently from financial assets. Margin debt is included in the broader accounting of household balance sheets in the FAD, but is excluded from the alignment with the BEA measure of NIPA saving. records.text: China Petchem Oil Demand Weakness Likely Mostly Unsustainable Drivers of Decline in China Demand The decline in China oil end-use demand has played a key role in reducing the global oil deficit and upward crude price pressure due to the Hormuz shock, offsetting over 15% of the Q2 hit to Persian Gulf production (Exhibit 1). We estimate that the fair value of crude prices based on OECD commercial stocks would have been about $15/bbl higher if China crude imports had not fallen. Given our base case assumption that Mideast output rises only gradually as shipping disruptions continue into 2027, a key question is whether China can continue to balance the market in this way. While we expect demand for gasoline and diesel to remain low as long as China product prices remain high, we see the decline in oil demand from the petrochemicals (“petchem”) sector as much less sustainable for two reasons. First, we estimate that nearly one-third of the Q2 0.40mb/d year-over-year (YoY) decline in China demand for oil products used in the petchem sector (i.e., naphtha, LPG, and ethane) already reversed by August. In contrast, diesel and gasoline demand remain very suppressed, having only recovered by 9% and 7% from their respective Q2 YoY declines of 0.31mb/d and 0.27mb/d (Exhibit 2). As AI capabilities continue to advance rapidly, elevated investment across the value chain has increased scrutiny around ROI. Even as the cost per unit of intelligence declines, broader adoption and the shift toward more complex and agentic workflows is driving enterprise spend higher. In response, companies are re-evaluating how AI is deployed from both a technology and application perspective, with a greater emphasis on controlling the intelligence stack and proven execution. Enterprise Spend Is Rising Despite Cost Declines Since publishing Positioning for AI Disruption (US Edition & EU Edition) earlier this year, the AI cost paradox has become more apparent. At the same time, the rise of open-weight models, including highly- capable Chinese models, has intensified competition. A more measured pace of tightening is needed to ensure smooth monetary policy transmission in a situation characterized by non-linear dynamics in debt markets. In such a situation, improving the degree of control of the financial conditions takes precedence over the aim of reducing the size of the balance sheet. There is no benchmark necessarily on what the final size of the ECB balance sheet needs to be or how fast the balance sheet needs to shrink. It is a self- imposed process. In addition, the ECB is approaching the €2.0 trillion mark of outstanding excess liquidity ahead of the year end, and for transmission purposes the Council might judge that a temporary pause in QT is needed. It would send a clear signal to the market that the ECB puts a premium on an orderly, controlled monetary tightening, a potentially very powerful message in current market conditions. We present below how much we could see from the ECB in terms of reinvestments given the PEPP/PSPP redemption profiles. We think the decision could come as early as in the October meeting - but some more tightening at the long end would be needed to push the ECB to that course of action.

Several commentators, including the Governor of the Bank of England, have stated that the precise timing of losses, and how they are accounted for on the combined public sector balance sheet (that brings together the Bank and the government) are simply a matter of accounting and not economically important. On one level, this is true. HM Treasury will ultimately bear the costs of the QE/QT programme. Whether losses are crystallised now through sales or later through maturing bonds should, in the long run, lead to a similar eventual loss, when discounted through time. And given HMT’s commitment to indemnify those losses, whether transfers to the APF are made now or in some future year only moves resources through time. However, to draw on the often-used sentiment from Keynes, in the long run we are all dead, and if economics is anything, it is the study of how to best allocate our resources not just across people and places, but also across time. Keeping the current arrangements is a choice to spend £20 billion per year on a transfer to the Bank of England now, rather than at a later date. This is similar to the choice the government faces when deciding whether to bear the costs of public spending now through taxation, or to borrow now and finance them through future taxation. Key components to watch 1. Airfares: How much more? Airfares remain the core category most directly affected by higher oil prices. Airfare CPI is already up 23% y/y, which raises the question of how much further prices can increase. One useful benchmark is the increase in airline operating costs resulting from higher jet fuel prices, as it provides a rough estimate of the fare adjustment needed to keep profit margins unchanged. Jet fuel prices have risen nearly 90% y/y and typically account for roughly 20-30% of airline operating costs. This implies a fuel-related cost shock of approximately 18-27%. By that metric, airlines may already be approaching full pass-through of the increase in fuel costs to consumers. Does that imply a deceleration in airfare inflation ahead? Possibly, and that is why we expect softer prints ahead – closer to the 0%m/m mark. However, if tensions in the Middle East intensify and oil prices rise further, airfare inflation is likely to remain elevated and could move even higher in y/y terms.

The French Government bond market has come under extreme pressure recently, with developments there drawing comparisons with the Eurozone crisis of 2011–12. One way to empirically assess whether UK gilt yields are experiencing greater pressure than the bonds of other governments is to examine how closely they move with respect to moves in other major bond markets. The relationship between the yields on a specific UK bond (e.g. a 30- year gilt) and a bond in another market (e.g. a 30-year US Treasury) is commonly referred to as a ‘beta’ . This measure guides market participants as to how much they should expect gilt yields to move given a move in other core markets. A beta greater than +1 means that gilt yields have tended to move by more than yields in the comparator market. This would imply, for example, that in a sell-off, gilt yields move higher by a greater amount and thereby underperform in the sell-off. Over the last 12 months, and as shown in Figure 6, the betas against a range of comparators have fallen, suggesting that the UK is not coming under the pressure that we had seen in previous episodes of global fixed income discontent. Given the recent market focus, we provide some historical perspective on France’s external position (current account) and how it compares with Italy, Spain and the United States. Going into the GFC, Spain ran the largest current account deficit and ultimately received financial assistance from the EFSF/ESM. Italy ran a more modest current account deficit going into the GFC. Both countries have since undergone macroeconomic adjustments, which are now resulting in positive current account positions. Household resilience built over the boom Household balance sheets remain resilient despite the cash rate rising 100bp in 2026 to 4.6%, a 15-year high. According to the RBA, fewer than 2% of variable-rate owner- occupier borrowers are currently experiencing a cash flow shortfall. This strength reflects years of house price gains, moderate growth in liabilities, and a still-tight labour market supporting incomes, although the recent housing downturn is likely to gradually erode some of these wealth gains. Liquidity buffers for a rainy day The key buffer behind this resilience is liquidity. This resilience is broad-based, with the median mortgage prepayment buffer larger than pre- pandemic levels across all income quartiles. While this strength is broad-based, borrowers with high loan-to-value and loan-to-income ratios continue to show higher arrears than the broader market. Why rely on market rates that the Fed doesn’t control instead of using the policy tools that it does? There also seems to be some asymmetry here. Would the Fed interpret a rally at the long end as a sign that it needs to tighten even more? Or would it conclude that markets are pricing a policy mistake? Probably the latter. The Fed risks falling behind the curve In our view, the cons of pausing outweigh the pros. The nominal economy is booming and there is substantial risk that the energy shock will pass through to core and food prices in coming months. The laundry list of inflation concerns in the September minutes suggests the Fed is well aware of the upside risks to inflation. But it doesn’t seem to think that they warrant rate hikes at the same cadence as last year’s cuts. If policymakers have already decided to stay on hold in Oct, before even seeing the Sep inflation data, they are taking the risk that y/y inflation could meaningfully accelerate over the next three months (Sep-Nov). Especially given that the base effects are unfavorable (Exhibit 2). Markets would likely then price i) an accelerated tightening cycle, and ii) higher breakeven inflation and/or term premium due to concerns about Fed credibility. What have survey data told us for August? The services PMI jumped to 52.5 in August, recording its highest print in four months. New work was also up for a second month. The CBI Growth Indicator , however, painted a more negative picture, with private -sector activity coming in at -23 in the three months to August (slipping from -21 in the three months to July). The BDO’s latest Business Trends survey , however, saw its o utput index jump to its highest level since January 2025, led by the services sector. And consumer sentiment improved on the margins through summer. Looking at the underlying detail, we see a mixed bag of data. On the plus side, we expect retail and wholesale sales volumes to have expanded in August. Retail sales (including autos) jumped by 0.5% m-o-m, recording its second highest level since April 2022. records.text: Regional markets’ macro sensitivity has moderated as importance of tech has n increased The dominant profit and index cap share of technology is changing the way the region’s equity markets trade macro variables. The r-square or ‘goodness of fit’ of our macro model has dropped from a fairly persistent 50-80% range over the past two decades to 30% at present. This shows that investors cannot simply use a top-down framework to determine their regional equity views. Instead, they should now use a hybrid approach which includes the macro backdrop together with sector-specific analysis, most notably of info tech. This is underscored by the high correlation of the equal-weight regional index with our AI basket, i.e. the region is currently trading more in line with micro than macro variables. More broadly, the r-squares of individual regional markets and sectors to key macro variables such as US economic growth, US rates, and commodity prices differ meaningfully, supporting the argument for a more granular approach to investing in Asian equities. records.text: European Economic Perspectives 8 October 2026 ab 12 Box: The budget process in France Article 47 of the French Constitution imposes the obligation to pass a budget in time for the following year by the end of the current year, with a strict time frame. However, the Constitution includes various safeguards that aim to ensure budget continuity and prevent a US-style government shutdown, whereby the government would no longer be allowed to pay its bills; see here, here and here for details. To start, a draft budget needs to be sent to parliament in time to allow for approval, and parliament has 70 days to vote on the budget bill (40 days for a first reading in the National Assembly, 15 days in the Senate, and the remaining time to find agreement between both chambers). To ensure a budget is in place at the start of the following year, this time frame implies that the budget draft has to be sent to parliament by 6 October 2026 (first Tuesday in October). This allows parliament to adopt the budget by mid-December. Before being promulgated, Art. 61 of the Constitution allows the budget bill to be referred to the Constitutional Council at the request of 60 deputies or 60 senators (as well as the President of the Republic, the Prime Minister, or the presidents of the assemblies). In case the 70-day period is not respected, and no bill is voted before the end of the year, the Constitution distinguishes between whether this delay is due to parliament or the government. The conflict has pushed inflation back up and it has now been above the Bank of England’s target for five years. Central banks have kept interest rates higher for longer than previously expected and this has pushed the cost of borrowing up for both the government and firms. FX: AI adds to the CNY’s external anchor The most direct FX transmission comes through the trade balance. AI-related exports now represent a significant share of China’s exports, making China an important manufacturing beneficiary of the global AI capital-expenditure cycle. This should generate additional foreign- currency receipts and reinforce the structural support to the CNY from China’s large trade surplus. However, the CNY response is unlikely to be proportional to the export boost. The conversion of export receipts into CNY will remain important, particularly as exporters may retain part of their foreign-currency earnings or use them to finance imported equipment and overseas investment. Moreover, the AI export cycle remains closely linked to foreign demand and capital expenditure by overseas hyperscalers. As the global AI capital-expenditure cycle eventually normalises, the boost to China’s exports and growth is also likely to moderate. There is also a policy constraint on appreciation. With domestic demand remaining weak and exports accounting for most of the AI growth dividend, policymakers have an incentive to preserve external competitiveness. records.text: iscal Source: Insee, Morgan Stanley Research estimates Debt rapidly on the rise with unchanged policy: Unsurprisingly, in our expansionary fiscal scenario with an unchanged primary deficit close to 3% of GDP, the debt ratio increases very rapidly, at a pace of 4pp per annum and towards almost 180% of GDP in 2040 (Exhibit 10). Maybe less intuitively, our "base case", which assumes a relatively significant consolidation, does not prevent debt increasing rapidly, towards almost 160% of GDP in 2040. Lastly, by construction, only the fiscal consolidation of €150Bn of our "conservative" scenario allows the debt ratio to stabilize. Much higher interest payments: We also note that in all our scenarios, interest payments increase meaningfully (Exhibit 11), and, while interest payments are today a relatively low share of GDP and below what was observed in the early 2000's (3%), this will not last. This is actually relatively straightforward to understand as they reflect higher yields on a debt that amounts to more than 100% of GDP. But we think an interesting result is that even in our most favourable scenario, interest payments would amount to more than 6% of GDP. We note on top that, in that scenario, with a primary surplus of 2% of GDP, the headline deficit would remains above 4%. More consolidation would actually be needed to keep the deficit below 3%.

records.text: 2027 Default Rates: Higher Risk Within The Left Tail The move higher in global yields has been accompanied by wider HY credit spreads, creating a dual headwind for firms needing to refinance in the near term. Since the start of the year, the all-in yield on the Bloomberg USD HY index has risen by approximately 170bp, to 8.3%, including a 40bp increase in the credit spread component relative to underlying Treasury yields. In Europe, the all-in yield on the Bloomberg EUR HY index has increased by roughly 140bp, to 7.3%, including a 60bp rise relative to similar-maturity Bund yields. In other words, the increase in all-in refinancing costs has been more pronounced than the move in risk-free rates alone would suggest, particularly in the EUR market. With this in mind, we outline our default expectations for 2027 across HY bonds and leveraged loans in both the USD and EUR markets. Broadly speaking, we expect the rise in refinancing costs to keep pressure on the left tail of the credit distribution (where firms generally have thinner financial cushions). Note: Throughout this piece, we are using our issuer-weighted default series, which includes distressed exchanges. While the mid- to upper-income demographics are benefiting from the net wealth effect, there is still evidence of differentiation in what money is being spent on, and on the lower end of the income spectrum, worsening inflationary pressure is having a greater effect. This is resulting in a tale of two sectors as we look across the consumer products side (which manufactures them) and the retail side (which sells them). Retailers have largely remained resilient, buoyed by tariff refunds, which have been used to reinvest behind price in order to drive traffic trends with consumers (see 2Q26 Earnings: Tariff Flow-Through). Resilient performance reflects disciplined lending and a supportive labor market Consumer ABS performance has remained resilient in 2026, and we expect continued stability in delinquency and net loss trends into early 2027, supported by disciplined underwriting, only modest growth in consumer debt, and a broadly healthy labor market. Banks have maintained stable-to-tighter lending standards across consumer products since the beginning of 2025 (Figure 7). Consumer debt growth has remained modest at roughly 2.5–3% y/y, and household balance sheets have benefited from strong wealth creation, with net worth increasing by nearly $13trn during H1 26 (Figure 8). Continued strength in consumer spending also provides comfort, as a spending pullback would likely precede weaker credit trends. Credit card utilization is another potential early-warning indicator, but neither aggregate data nor card ABS trusts show meaningful deterioration (Figure 9). Headline consumer credit metrics likely overstate underlying weakness, in our view. Specifically, the New York Fed’s quarterly report on household debt and credit stock delinquency rates includes balances that have already been charged off by lenders but continue to appear in credit bureau statistics. After adjusting for these charged-off balances, consumer credit performance appears considerably more stable with transition rates in 30+ day delinquency stabilizing or improving

In some regions, concerns about AI itself, including job displacement, security risks, and a lack of trust in large technology companies, are beginning to emerge alongside more traditional environmental and infrastructure concerns. This is creating growing tension between national AI ambitions and the interests of the communities expected to host the infrastructure. International expansion is not always a viable solution. Moving AI infrastructure into jurisdictions such as Canada, Mexico, or other foreign markets introduces questions around data sovereignty, national security, regulatory oversight, and legal jurisdiction. Governments and enterprises increasingly want sensitive data, AI models, and critical digital infrastructure to remain under domestic control, particularly as AI becomes more strategically important. records.text: The rise in global yields has been accompanied by wider HY credit spreads, n creating a dual headwind for firms approaching refinancing. Since the start of the year, USD HY all-in yields have risen by roughly 170bp, to 8.3%, while EUR HY all-in yields have increased by approximately 140bp, to 7.3%. In our view, the key issue for default risk is not the absolute level of yields, but rather where refinancing needs, weaker capital structures and sector-specific pressures overlap. We favor USD HY over EUR HY, as we expect the EUR market to remain more n vulnerable in 2027. We forecast the US HY 12-month trailing default rate to rise modestly to around 4% (vs. 3.3% as of September), but remain slightly below its long-run average. By contrast, we expect the EUR HY default rate to remain around 5%, above its long-run average. A steeper maturity wall, higher refinancing costs for CCCs and greater overlap between upcoming maturities and energy-sensitive and consumer sectors should keep the EUR default cycle more extended. Our regional preference is reversed in leveraged loans, where we favor the EUR n market over its USD peer. We forecast the USD leveraged loan default rate to remain elevated at around 5% in 2027, above its long-run average. EUR leveraged loan defaults should also rise, to around 4% in 2027 (vs. 2.7% as of September), well above the historical average of less than 2%. These occur when the APF sells a bond to the market (active unwind) and reflect the difference between the price paid for the bond originally – the initial proceeds amount - and the price at which the bond is sold. Conceptually this is because the APF receives the current price of the bond from the market, but must pay back a portion of the loan it owes the Bank equal to what it borrowed to buy the bond in the first place. As with maturity losses, this loss does not affect day-to-day government spending in the current budget, but it does add to public sector debt. A key difference is the timing. As the eventual sale price is not known when the APF first buys the bond, the sales gain or loss only adds to PSND and PSNFL in the year the bond is sold. Where there are losses, the cash transfer to the APF – the sum of these three losses – does have to be funded. It adds, all else equal, to the government’s net cash requirement. As well as the direct fiscal implications of transfers relating to the QE/QT programme, there are also indirect consequences for the government’s finances. The QE programme increased demand for government bonds and so reduced yields and government borrowing costs, although this was not the primary aim of the policy. QE was used to support the economy after the 2009 global financial crisis, the 2016 Brexit shock and in response to the 2020 pandemic-induced slowdown. The APF’s bond holdings peaked in 2021 when it owned £875 billion in gilts (around a third of total government debt) and a further £20 billion in UK corporate bonds (Ramsden, 2023). QE was intended to be a temporary intervention. Since 2022, the Bank of England has been ‘unwinding’ it, reducing the stock of bonds it holds in the APF. This has become known as quantitative tightening, or QT . The Bank has carried out quantitative tightening in two ways. First, it has allowed some bonds to reach maturity. When this happens, the APF receives the redemption value from the bond issuer and pays back the initial loan it took out from the Bank of England. This is termed passive unwind. Second, it has sold some bonds on the market. The APF receives the going market price for the bond and pays back the initial loan it took out from the Bank of England, which in turn, reduces the reserve balance of commercial banks, all else equal. These are called active sales, or active unwind. How do QE and QT lead to financial flows between HM Treasury and the Asset Purchase Facility? This distinction is important because it suggests fiscal slippage (a worsening fiscal out-turn compared with forecasts or expectations) alone can be viewed as a necessary but not sufficient condition for a bond market crisis. Rather, the credibility shock of weakening or unsustainable fiscal policy becomes dangerous when it interacts with existing financial system vulnerabilities. If we frame the LDI crisis in this way, the September 2022 gilt crisis appears to have been an idiosyncratic UK event driven by a combination of fiscal policy errors and structural vulnerabilities in the UK pension system. For policymakers, the key lesson is not that bond vigilantes are perennially poised to punish fiscally profligate governments, but that institutional credibility, hidden leverage and financial sector vulnerabilities matter enormously. It would be a reach to think that the episode in 2022 triggered a lasting rejection of UK government debt. Discretionary appetite for gilts has remained solid. But it did give rise to an impression of fiscal vulnerability that has proven nigh on impossible to shake off. Lastly, in case of any other rejection of the budget law not foreseen by legislation, such as a systematic rejection of the budget bill or emergency measures, a Constitutional Council ruling from 1978 could apply. This requires the government and parliament to find a solution to ensure the functioning of the state, in essence by extending the previous year's budget. As a very last resort, the Constitution's Art. 16 grants the president exceptional powers in case "the institutions of the Republic, the independence of the Nation, the integrity of its territory or the fulfilment of its international commitments are under serious and immediate threat, and where the proper functioning of the constitutional public authorities is interrupted". During the three-month interval, 2s5s IRS bear-flattened meaningfully, almost for the first time since the BoJ’s lift-off in 2024 from its negative interest rate policy . The magnitude of the flattening was a sharp 15bp if measured from the bear-steepening during the ‘Basic Policy shock’, or a still-decent 5bp if measured from the BoJ’s meeting on 16 June (Figure 1). As the current 44bp still feels quite steep for 2s5s under tightening environment compared with other G3 curves, it is tempting to think that the 2s5s can bear-flatten further if the BoJ has finally become serious about a faster– like quarterly – pace of rate hikes especially if a terminal rate of 2% has to be reached by Q2 2027. But we take a cautious view and favour entering a 2s5s steepener, hedged by paying 1y or 9m IRS, mainly based on a comparison with other G3 (USD and EUR) curves. Historical moves: Other than the above noted bear-flattening, the only time the 2s5s bear-flattened was a very brief move just before the BoJ’s lift-off from NIRP in March 2024 (Figure 2). In Q1 2025, even though the BoJ became confident about CPI and wage growth after the Q1 2025 hike (to 0.50%), 2s5s simply bear-steepened. At that time, the BoJ’s terminal rate was generally thought to be in the 1% range. It is indeed a meaningful change for the BoJ to have hiked even to the current policy rate of 1.25% while still maintaining a hiking stance. BOND WATCH Chile bonds flows stand out Figure 6 Chile bond flows Foreign investors have continued to add to Chilean local bonds in recent months despite the rise in developed market yields, highlighting confidence in the country's macroeconomic framework. Chile's monetary policy remains well anchored, while public debt at around 45% of GDP underscores the strength of its balance sheet. The incoming administration's plans to front -load fiscal consolidation should further support debt sustainability over the medium term. These strong fundamentals are particularly valuable as the economy navigates stagflationary pressures stemming from higher oil prices and adverse weather conditions. In turn, they provide the central bank with greater scope to decouple from the Fed's hawkish stance and keep policy rates lower for longer. This backdrop is more supportive for bonds than for FX, and we believe the recent bond inflows, which appear largely hedged, still have room to continue. Both countries have similar primary deficits somewhat above 2.5% of GDP, but the US has a higher interest bill, so its headline deficit (c 6% of GDP) is higher than France’s (c 5% of GDP). It is worth noting, however, that fiscal numbers are not directly comparable given methodological differences across countries. In both cases, social spending and entitlements is a significant fraction of total spending, making spending commitments very sticky and politically costly to reverse— with some consolidation attempts even failing due to social unrest. Therefore, structural increases in spending require a permanent level of revenues of similar magnitude for fiscal policy to be sustainable. Countries differ significantly though in the size of the government. Public spending in France is more than 50% of GDP, roughly 20pp higher than in the US. In both countries, the post pandemic deficit increases were primarily driven by lower revenues more so than by higher spending. Interestingly, both countries enjoyed a significant revenue boost during 2021-2022, followed by a significant drop after 2022, although the drivers were completely different. Our estimates indicate that the BoJ’s share of JGB holdings will decline significantly, from above 50% currently to around 20% by 2035. However, surveys of bond market participants suggest that supply-demand factors are not receiving particularly high attention and are not generally regarded as the primary driver of recent increases in long-term interest rates. Overall, we believe the key factors supporting higher long-term yields have limited further upside, implying that Japanese long-term rates are unlikely to rise substantially from current levels. Indeed, our model-based estimate of the 10-year yield, excluding the fiscal risk premium, currently stands at around 3.0%, broadly consistent with prevailing market levels. So, if sovereign spreads have overshot fundamentals, the discount applied to internationally diversified French companies may also be excessive. Relative cheapness is not yet a catalyst. Alternative ways of managing and accounting for the costs of QT going forward Given the importance of how these flows are distributed across people and time, a number of alternative arrangements have been discussed that would result in a different set of allocations. One often discussed proposal aims to reduce the near-term costs of the policy by slowing the unwind of the gilt holdings in the APF . As highlighted by the analysis above, this reduces, or even removes the sales losses, but elongates both the interest rate losses and maturity losses. In fact, if the entire gilt portfolio were held to maturity, with only passive unwind, HM Treasury would still be covering losses as far into the future as 2071. This problem is particularly acute in the UK compared with its peers as the average maturity of government borrowing in the UK is much longer. This proposal amounts to a shift of the cost burden through time, pushing more of it into the future. The essence of this proposal has largely been enacted by the Bank of England as part of its September announcement. The different versions of the USD Forward Volatility strategies aim to capture the positive carry on the 3m10y20y forward volatility when the rates volatility curve is downward-sloping, by taking a long position on USD 10y20y and USD 3m10y swaptions as well as a short position on USD 3m30y via delta-hedged straddles. By doing that, the strategies have a long vega exposure – positive sensitivity to a change in the implied volatility. Gamma neutral (BNPXLVGU): The notional of the 3M30Y and 3M10Y swaptions are scaled to remove the gamma sensitivity of the 10Y20Y. Notional weighted (BNPXLVNU): The notional on the different swaption legs is the same, resulting in a short gamma exposure in addition to the long vega exposure. Notional weighted with trend (BNPXLWNU): This adds a long trend exposure by hedging the delta on the long legs only when it exceeds a certain level in absolute terms. records.text: 2 Euro Area Viewpoint | 09 October 2026 France External (im)balances: not a very large twin deficit Thinking back to 2011, large public deficits and large current account deficits, aka “twin deficits”, come to mind. In France, that is not so much the case. True, the current account is more often in deficit than not, but the imbalance is small – 0.6% of GDP on average since 2006. Large public sector deficits, similar today to their 2011 levels, are almost matched by private sector surpluses – households in particular (Exhibit 1). That can still create mismatches, of course. Unlike in Italy, France doesn’t have a “retail” version of the OAT, and that is perhaps not easy to create from scratch, especially in the midst of market turmoil. Plus, many years of a small current account deficit still led to a net international investment position of -29% of GDP (Exhibit 2). “Debt securities”, incl OATs, are the bulk of that and, if sold, could increase France’s challenge. The AFT (Agence France Trésor) reports some 57% of outstanding negotiable sovereign debt to be held by non-residents. But compared to most Euro area peers (and even more so compared to Anglo-Saxon economies), France’s NIIP is relatively small. records.text: 2026 is on track to be a record year for US equity issuance. US corporates have n raised $431 billion YTD via IPOs, follow-ons, converts, and SPACs, representing growth of 98% year/year. The total dollar volume of US equity issuance in 2026 will likely surpass the previous high of $540 billion in 2021. However, the number of deals and the value of issuance scaled to market cap are close to historical averages. Following record issuance volumes in Q2, macro volatility has weighed on n activity in recent months. In addition to a handful of large deals, more than 90 US equity offerings came to market in each of May and June. However, the monthly average declined to roughly 50 deals in Q3. Sharp rises in interest rates have historically been associated with declining issuance volumes, and this pattern has been repeated recently. We expect corporate equity issuance will total $600 billion in 2027. Solid n economic growth, rising equity prices, a decline in interest rates, and ongoing AI investment should drive continued robust equity issuance in 2027. We forecast IPO volume of $175 billion and other primary supply of $425 billion. This issuance would collectively equate to 0.8% of US equity market cap, in line with the 10-year average. arket. 2026 is not a rerun of 2022 The most recent bout of bond market turbulence has inevitably resurrected the market’s collective memories of the events of the 2022 gilt/LDI crisis. LDI – liability-driven investments – are strategies that UK pension funds used to structure their investments in order to efficiently hedge liabilities. They are meant to ensure that the value of their assets and future pension entitlements move in step. However, the use of leverage and repo exposed pension funds to risk if gilts moved sharply. In the mini-Budget in September 2022, Chancellor Kwasi Kwarteng announced large unfunded tax cuts that implied much higher government borrowing. Gilt yields rose sharply. Pension funds had to find cash to cover the fall in the value of gilt collateral against which they had borrowed. In order to meet margin calls, they were forced to sell gilts and this triggered a doom loop of falling values and forced selling. The Bank of England had to step in to break the spiral as it judged that the moves posed a significant financial stability risk.2 It is understandable that the shadow of the LDI crisis still looms over the gilt market and, as we are frequently reminded, ‘those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it’ . But it would not be correct to think that UK institutions and policymakers have ignored the lessons from that experience – in fact, quite the opposite. We estimate that Persian Gulf liquids output recovered from 14.8mb/d below February 2026 levels in April to roughly 6mb/d below in September. Given September’s upside surprise, we modestly raise our base-case production path for Persian Gulf producers (Exhibit 10). We assume Mideast output returns gradually to pre-war levels by 2027H2 before overshooting as the UAE and Saudi Arabia deploy spare capacity. Although Gulf output is likely to be less smooth than our stylized base case, we expect it to trend higher as continued adaptation and added transportation resources—especially pipelines and a larger tanker fleet—support further gains. A September increase in tankers willing to exit the Gulf supported the recovery in oil production and exports of previously produced crude. We attribute the rise in Gulf exports mainly to greater adaptation and higher risk tolerance among producers and specialized shippers despite persistent shipping risks, supported by strong economic and national incentives and US military protection for transits. Productivity growth Offsetting declining labour force growth, we expect productivity – output per worker – growth to increase through the forecast from 0.6% per year in 2026 to 1.1% per year in 2031.3 There are two reasons output per worker is growing in our forecast. First, we expect investments in capital (e.g. buildings and equipment) to increase the stock of capital available to workers – ‘capital deepening’ . This makes each worker more productive as each worker can do more if they have more equipment available to them. We expect this effect to be a steady upward force throughout our forecast period. Second, we expect output per worker to increase as the technologies for translating a given set of capital and labour into output increase. In the near term, we expect cyclical influences that have weighed on productivity, such as labour hoarding post-pandemic and supply-side shocks, to subside and bolster productivity growth. We expect investments in new technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) to pay off and improve the economy’s ability to translate inputs into outputs going forward and for this technological growth to increase over time – from 0.1% per year in 2026 to 0.5% in 2031. Productivity growth is highly uncertain and different forecasters will take different views. And while the regional bank presidents were the most vocal around hikes during FOMC meetings, there has been a general hawkish shift in overall Fed speak since the start of the year. Figure 2 shows that our media readings of hawkishness vs dovishness of Fed coverage started to notably, and sustainably, tick up near the start of the Iran war and remained net hawkish since then. Unsurprisingly, inflation readings also moved aggressively to the upside during this period, particularly headline readings, which include the impact of higher food and energy costs. And while we have not seen the same degree of pass through of higher prices into core readings of inflation, the tightening bias remains, with media still net hawkish and the dots calling for yet another hike before year end. records.text: Italy—A De ficit Surprise Challenges the Debt Decline A Fiscal Surprise In the updated budgetary programme last Friday, the Italian government revised up its fiscal deficit targets for 2027 and 2028 by a cumulative 1.2% of GDP . This suggests that flexibility under the European fiscal rules granted by the activation of the National Escape Clause (NEC) will be used to raise the deficit rather than offset the consolidation otherwise required after exit from the Excessive Deficit Procedure, which we expect in April 2027. The deficit revision is split evenly between defence and energy-related measures, each worth 0.3% of GDP per year in 2027 and 2028, with final details due in the October budget; market participants, including us, view the new targets as a significant upward surprise versus the government’s April path (Exhibit 1). In the updated budgetary programme, the Italian government lifted its 2027/2028 deficit targets to 3.4%/3.2% of GDP , from 2.6%/2.4% before, and above our 2.9%/2.8% forecasts. As the European Recovery Fund’s support fades, the scale of the deficit revision implies that fiscal policy turns slightly expansionary in 2027, a notable shift from the drag observed in 2026 and previously expected for 2027 (Exhibit 2). This follows the observation that central banks usually stop hiking before inflation fully moderates. After the peak, yields tend to decline rapidly, falling on average by 40bp across the curve after the first year past the inflation peak, and more if benchmarking to the timing of the final hike. Based on historical patterns, our baseline that inflation will continue to moderate can be a source of relief as markets accumulate evidence. Confirmation that inflation is on a downward trajectory also tends to mark the end of more acute curve flattening. That said, it is only typically after hikes end that curves begin to steepen again. In the US, we found that the subsequent relief rally tends to be even more in parallel. This again underlines the value of outright longs over curve steepeners. Looking across episodes, 10y yields peaked around the time of the first hike and then started declining in three of the last five Fed hike cycles (Exhibit 4). However, these cycles (1997, 2004, and 2015) were characterized by different macro conditions at the onset of hikes. records.text: PM Sanchez has called early elections Since 2023, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has led a minority coalition government with the left- wing Sumar alliance, relying on ad hoc support from regional and pro-independence parties (Figure 1), a fragile parliamentary arrangement that has constrained the government's ability to pass major legislation. This ultimately prompted Sánchez to call a snap general election for 29 November, following the Congress of Deputies' rejection of two government decrees aimed at addressing Spain's housing crisis. Voters will elect both chambers of the national parliament (Cortes Generales): • Congress of Deputies (Congreso de los Diputados): all 350 seats are allocated by proportional representation (D'Hondt method), with closed party lists in 52 constituencies (the 50 provinces plus Ceuta and Melilla). • Senate (Senado): 208 seats are directly elected under a majority-vote system, while the remaining senators (58 in the outgoing legislature) are appointed by regional assemblies. Spain's constitution gives the Congress clear primacy over the Senate. Congress can override the Senate's objections, and it alone elects and can remove the Prime Minister. It is therefore the composition of the Congress that will determine government formation. To be confirmed, a candidate needs an absolute majority (176 votes) in a first vote or a simple majority (more votes in favour than against) in a second vote held 48 hours later. We build our base case on our analysts’ estimates and industry insights summarized above, and frame optimistic and cautious scenarios using a market-based approach of current high and low consensus estimates. Beyond 2028, we assume earnings growth gradually normalizes toward historical cycle (20-yr) averages, converging to 18% growth by 2032. Based on these assumptions, in our base case we project MXAPJ tech-sector earnings to grow at a 20% CAGR over 2027-31 from +260% in 2026, equivalent to roughly the 60th percentile of historical five-year earnings growth outcomes over the past two decades. The bull case implies 28% CAGR (85th percentile), while the bear case implies only 9% CAGR (18th percentile), primarily driven by a sharp downturn in memory earnings. And while the economy does not seem to be overheating, it is also not showing signs of stress, prompting the FOMC’s impatience on returning inflation to targets. records.text: Refreshing our 10-year earnings growth forecasts Building on our tech sector analysis, we refresh our long-term 10-year earnings growth forecasts we first introduced in our global strategy paper last year. To do so, we update our forecasts for 2026-2028 (years 0-2) and then model 2029-2036 (years 3-10) based on the historical relationship between earnings growth and GDP growth, while assuming that growth and margins gradually normalize toward long-term levels. We also explicitly model the year 3-4 transition for Taiwan and Korea to reflect our constructive views on AI-related fundamentals. For Taiwan, this incorporates our outlook on AI capex and industry supply-demand dynamics, which we believe will support above-cycle earnings growth. For Korea, we assume earnings growth moderates from an elevated base and margin level but remains positive rather than turning negative. For example, the Arabian Gulf-Japan freight index (Bloomberg: D27BAGJP BGAP Index) stood at around USD34/bbl on October 7, far above its normal level of roughly USD2/bbl ( Exhibit 7 ). The impact on Japan's crude import prices is likely to be smaller than implied by the increase in this index. The index reflects freight costs for cargoes loaded in the Persian Gulf, while freight rates for cargoes loaded in Fujairah or the United States are likely lower. In addition, most VLCCs operated by Japan's major shipping companies are under medium- to long-term contracts, limiting the pass-through of spot freight rate increases. Nevertheless, higher transportation costs could continue to push Japan's crude import prices higher, adding to the upward pressure already coming from rising futures prices.

records.text: European Economic Perspectives 8 October 2026 ab 13 What to expect from legislative elections? The extent to which the next president can implement his or her agenda − particularly with respect to passing budgets − will depend heavily on the composition of parliament. Without a parliamentary majority, any new president may become a "lame duck", at least on domestic matters. The next scheduled legislative elections are not due until June 2029, five years after the 2024 election. However, the traditional pattern under the Fifth Republic has been to hold legislative elections shortly after a presidential election. To do so in 2027, the newly elected president would need to dissolve the National Assembly, triggering elections within 20-40 days. If dissolution occurred immediately after taking office, legislative elections could take place as early as June 2027. Historically, presidential elections have often been followed either by a parliamentary majority aligned with the president − facilitating implementation of the government's programme, as during Macron's first term − or by a period of cohabitation, in which the opposition controls parliament and constrains the president's policy agenda, as under Jacques Chirac between 1997 and 2002. Since 2022, however, no party or bloc has secured an outright majority, forcing successive prime ministers to rely on fragile minority governments. records.text: Exporter conversions: supportive, but less likely to accelerate Exporter conversion flows should remain an underlying source of CNY support, but they are unlikely to provide the same impulse if expectations become less one-sided. Our view is that conversions should moderate as appreciation expectations become less uniform. This should create a stabilising feedback loop. When USDCNY is falling rapidly, weaker fixings and greater uncertainty over the authorities’ tolerance may discourage exporters from rushing to convert dollars. If the move stalls or reverses, exporters may use the higher USDCNY level to convert FX, limiting the extent of depreciation. The result should be a more gradual and self-correcting currency path. Exporter conversions can reinforce the policy floor when USDCNY rises, but fixing resistance should limit the risk that conversion flows generate a disorderly decline in the pair. We remain constructive on CNY, but expect a low-volatility grind rather than a one-way appreciation cycle. 9 October 2026 4 Barclays | FX & Economic Insights

Our key conclusions are as follows (discussed in more detail overleaf, where we also update key charts and tables). First, France's 2027 draft budget targets a deficit of 5.0% of GDP, supported by a €54bn (1.8% of GDP) fiscal consolidation package combining spending restraint and tax increases, including an extension of the corporate tax surcharge on large firms. However, the planned adjustment falls short of what is required under EU fiscal rules, implying that public debt will continue to rise and that France will likely remain dependent on European Commission flexibility. Second, given the political uncertainty ahead of the 2027 presidential election, the budget should be viewed as largely provisional. Any government taking office after next year's elections may revise the budget through a supplementary bill. The more immediate question is whether a budget can be passed at all. Our base case is that opposition parties ultimately allow a budget to pass before year-end, potentially through constitutional procedures that circumvent a parliamentary vote. As a tactical trade into the meeting, we recommend a 3m2y receiver spread financed by selling a payer. Our economists expect no change in October or December and the next hike in January, so none of their hikes falls inside the window of a 3m option, which expires in early January. The options market is paying for the same place: 3m2y implied vol stands at 55.4bp, up sha rply from 42.6bp at the end of July and at the 98th percentile since 2024, and 1m2y implied vol translates into a daily move of about 2.5bp, 1.7 times an ordinary day and more than the average move on BoJ decision days (2.2bp). Meanwhile the 2y rate three months forward is 2.06%, about 15bp above spot. We therefore buy a 2.06% receiver and sell a 1.81% receiver and a 2.31% payer. records.text: 9 October 2026 Focus Europe Deutsche Bank AG Page 4 Figure 5: Timetable for the 29 Nov general election Source: Deutsche Bank Research, Boletin Oficial del Estado Economy: Policy changes unlikely to derail robust growth The Spanish economy has proven resilient to political uncertainty in recent years and remains one of the fastest growing euro area member states : growth was 2.9% on average over 2023-2025, three times the growth rate of the euro area. Strong growth has continued in 2026. GDP expanded by 0.6% qoq in Q1-26 and 0.7% in Q2, compared to 0.3% qoq in both quarters for the euro area excluding Ireland. Domestic demand continues to be the primary driver of growth ( Figure 6). Household consumption has held up well despite inflation rising rapidly, from 2.4% yoy at the start of the year to 5.1% in Sep-26 (Figure 7). Investment continues to be supported by the deployment of NGEU funds. The latest business surveys points to continued robust activity heading into the autumn, with services PMI at its strongest level since early 2023. records.text: M Idea 10 Financial conditions: The Fed awakens Following the 25bp rate hike in September and the shift into an "oil risk premium" baseline, we reset our financial conditions index to September 15, 2026, the day prior to the September FOMC meeting, to track our FRB/US-based measure of financial conditions in this new hiking cycle. As of the October 8 market close, financial conditions were 32bp tighter than they were before the September FOMC meeting. The index aims to capture how changes in asset prices weigh on future economic activity. It includes five daily variables: the 10-year Treasury yield, S&P 500 returns, the corporate BBB credit spread, the valuation of the U.S. dollar, and the price of oil. These are aggregated based on their estimated growth elasticities relative to the federal funds rate using the Federal Reserve's FRB/US model. As a result, the index can be interpreted as the equivalent change in the federal funds rate, expressed in basis points, required to generate a similar effect on economic activity. Since the day before the September FOMC meeting, the easing in financial conditions has been equivalent to about a 33bp hike in the federal funds rate, driven primarily by a higher 10-year Treasury yield and USD appreciation. Equity returns and BBB credit spreads have offset some of the tightening. However, there is no clear end in sight, and many financial market participants are nervous that downward-sloping gas and oil futures curves – capturing that buyers are currently willing to pay more for near-dated contracts than for energy delivered further in the future – may be giving a false signal about the ultimate trajectory of prices. Delivered crude prices have returned to their spring highs, refinery margins are once again turning negative in Europe, and the risk of refinery run cuts is rising. Yet the forces driving the market are fundamentally different. In April, the problem was a shortage of crude. In October, it is the cost of moving it. The latest dislocation began in September, when Middle Eastern producers began moving more oil through the Strait of Hormuz. Flows jumped from around 7.5 mbd in July and August to 12 mbd in September, drawing an increasing number of tankers into the region. By September, 766 of the global fleet of 923 very large crude carriers (VLCCs) were in active use, leaving remarkably little spare capacity to absorb additional demand, particularly as 124 vessels within that fleet were effectively unavailable due to the US blockade of Iranian oil. The problem is not simply how many tankers are available, but how efficiently they can be used. The “Gap” Approach: Likely neutral, at most modestly restrictive Our assessment of the neutral policy rate starts by estimating the economy's underlying degree of slack using a multivariate unobserved-components framework, which jointly decomposes output, labor market and inflation indicators into permanent trends and a common cyclical component. We extend this framework by adding an interest-rate channel that allows the same system to infer the neutral real policy rate. Since 1Q25, our estimate of the real neutral policy rate has risen from a bit below 100bp to about 150bp. A real neutral rate of 1.5% would imply a nominal neutral rate of 3.5% if inflation were consistent with the 2% target, or 3.8–4.1% based on our current forecast for PCE inflation in 2027. Hence, the previous policy rate setting at 3.50–3.75% and the current setting of 3.75–4.00% would be viewed as neutral to moderately restrictive. Our estimate is within the range of other publicly available estimates, but there are two important caveats. First, neutral-rate estimates are inherently imprecise because r* is unobservable and must be inferred from other estimated variables. records.text: US Rates Weekly 09 October 2026 Citi Research 10 In Figure 21 we show the evolution of Fed liquidity (which we define as reserves plus RRP usage) as a percent to bank assets, in the six months before and after the debt ceiling resolution. As the figure shows, in some debt ceiling episodes Fed liquidity was declining into the resolution (as was the case in 2018 and 2019), while in other episodes it was increasing, like in 2021. In 2027 we anticipate that liquidity will be somewhat increasing into the debt ceiling resolution (see Figure 22). We pencil in around 15% as a percentage of bank assets; therefore, we don’t think 2021 makes a good analogue. We expect a late 2027 debt ceiling resolution, although we see a risk of a temporary deal that could push the resolution to early 2028. Therefore, we see some scope for 1y spreads to cheapen slightly in Q3 or Q4 next year, perhaps 5bp to 10bp, as we near the resolution of the debt ceiling. Once the debt ceiling is resolved, Treasury tends to quickly replenish the TGA balance by ramping up T-bill issuance. This quick increase in collateral funding needs plus the pullback in reserves from the increasing TGA balance tend to pressure repo rates higher. However, we think the Fed could temporarily buy T-bills to ease this potential upwards pressure on repo markets, so we expect front-end spreads to remain largely anchored then as well. Figure 22. records.text: These increases in gas, electricity, petrol and diesel prices are the direct impact of the energy price shock. The second key question for the inflation outlook is whether rising energy prices will lead to broader increases in prices for other goods and services. One potential channel for the energy price shock leading to broader inflation is through rising input costs for non-energy products. These are often termed indirect energy effects. However, so far we see little evidence of this. As shown in Figure 5, a measure of energy-intensive core inflation (which strips out direct energy bills, pump prices and also volatile food, alcohol and tobacco, but focuses on the goods and services where energy is a key input) remains around 2%. These are the goods and services where we would first expect to see any spillovers occurring from changes in direct energy costs. This effect is likely to build over time, and we expect a mild acceleration in the coming months but, eight months into the energy shock, we find it reassuring that there are still few signs of pressure in these groups. We think the pre-measures headroom has been lowered by ~£14bn to ~£10bn from £23.6bn in March (Exhibit 17). The key elements are: 1) Higher yields and Bank Rate expectations: £10bn hit In its conditioning assumptions, the OBR takes the Bank Rate and Gilt curve over 10 working days to a cutoff date, which is usually a month and a half before the Budget. In the 3 March ‘26 Spring forecasts, the OBR used the curve during 10 working days to 30 January for its fiscal forecasts (i.e. 5 weeks before). In our base case we use 10 working days to 25 Sept, which would be five weeks before 28 Oct. During 10 days to 25 Sept, 10-year yields were ~65bps higher in the near term and ~50bps higher in 2029-30 compared to the OBR’s March forecasts, which can lower the headroom by ~£6bn. Bank Rate expectations were 60-120bps higher in the near term and 80bps higher in 2029-30 compared to OBR’s March forecast, which can lower the headroom by ~£4bn. The OBR has the flexibility to adjust the window if it judges the need to capture important developments, which can affect the calculations. Overall, we estimate a £10bn hit to the headroom from higher interest payments. 2) Higher inflation: £3bn hit The OBR forecasts inflation at 2.3% in 2026 and 2.0% in 2027-30. We aggregate plants together to get monthly capacity lost and total capacity by production process. Overall we expect tax rises worth £8bn (0.3% of GDP) by 2029-30 to be announced to partially restore the post-measures headroom to £17bn (down from £23.6bn in March). There is uncertainty on the size of tax rises needed as it’s unclear what level of headroom the government is targeting. Reports suggest that the Chancellor is less willing to engage in large tax rises to fully restore the headroom. At the same time, a small headroom can increase focus on the government’s fiscal position due to a lower buffer for future shocks. We think that the government would want to target a level between £15-20bn, so we assume a midpoint of £17bn post-measures headroom. Expected policy measures On the spending side… We expect discretionary spending measures, costing £7-8bn in the near term and £2bn in 2029-30 to be announced (Exhibit 4). Non-Fed investors should have slightly over $250bn of coupon payments to reinvest next year, so if the coupon payments simply go back to MBS and we get the demand we expect from a few investors, then we think mortgages will be in a good spot. The issue is that investors have looked back and wonder if we are heading towards a repeat of 2022/2023 periods - will the Fed need to hike much more than the market is pricing in if they want to curtail activity enough to really slow expectation? Our economists don't think that's the case, but they estimate a 30% chance of an aggregate demand shock/animal spirits where the Fed has to hike rates to 5-5.25%. If that happens, mortgages will likely struggle materially. In most of the rest of their possibilities, we would expect mortgages to do well. Third, looking beyond the current budget, Marine Le Pen's fiscal plans are increasingly important, as she is leading in the polls. Her programme combines costly measures such as lowering the retirement age and cutting taxes with ambitious commitments to reduce the deficit through a "golden fiscal rule" and €140bn (4.7% of GDP) in planned cumulative spending cuts. We view these savings estimates cautiously, however, as they would require an unprecedented multi-year fiscal adjustment and rely in part on politically contentious measures, including a sharp reduction in France's contribution to the EU budget. Fourth, we view a rapid and pre-emptive ECB intervention in French bond markets as unlikely. Not least because of concerns about moral hazard, the Governing Council would probably require a much sharper deterioration in financing conditions or evidence of broader Eurozone contagion before considering activation of the TPI. Our rates strategists do not see country spreads returning to early September levels easily, see more details in this note as well as this note by our credit strategists. records.text: Japan Macro Watch 9 October 2026 ab 3 Will long-term interest rates rise further? Japanese long-term interest rates have risen sharply in recent months. The 10-year JGB yield climbed to 3.1% last week, its highest level in roughly three decades. While long- term yields have trended upward alongside progress in inflation-driven monetary normalization, the question is whether further significant increases lie ahead. In our view, a comprehensive assessment of the factors affecting long-term rates, including the policy-rate outlook, U.S. Treasury yields, and the fiscal risk premium, suggests that the scope for additional upward pressure is limited. Even if yields continue to rise, we expect the upside to be capped at around 3.3%. 1. Limited upside to terminal-rate expectations The market-implied terminal rate, as measured by the one-year OIS rate two years forward, currently stands at 2.5%, well above both the BoJ-watcher consensus of 1.75% and our forecast of 2.0%. A level of 2.5% is already near the upper end of the BoJ’s estimated neutral-rate range of 1.1%-2.5%. Further increases in terminal-rate expectations would imply that monetary policy is moving into restrictive territory. However, the risks of an accelerating wage-price spiral or the BoJ falling behind the curve on FX developments do not appear significant at present.
